text:
**Engineering Wednesday**

Identity theft and the fraud that comes with it are a documented problem in the two countries that supply most of the H-1B pipeline.

Turning our high trust society into a low trust society one visa at a time...

India ranked first among surveyed countries in 2022 for adult identity-theft victims, with an estimated 27.2 million. TransUnion measured India’s suspected digital fraud rate at 7.1 percent in 2025, nearly double the global average of 3.8 percent. Account login was the highest-risk stage. Sophos found that about 77 percent of surveyed organizations in India experienced at least one identity-related breach in the prior year. Large secondary datasets of Aadhaar and related identifiers have repeatedly shown up for sale on dark-web forums. Indian police have opened cases where stolen or forged Aadhaar and PAN documents were used for tens of crores in fraudulent transactions. UIDAI has deactivated more than 20 million “ghost” Aadhaar numbers tied to deceased persons after cross-checking death registries.

China’s Enforcement Directorate investigations in India have traced Chinese nationals as the main operators behind most illegal instant loan apps and related crypto scams. The apps offer short-term loans through mobile phones, require broad access to contacts, photos, and other phone data, then use that data for blackmail and harassment when borrowers miss the high-interest, short-term terms. The ED has identified roughly Rs 28,000 crore in crime proceeds from these networks. China-linked contractors and groups have also been documented pulling large volumes of foreign identity data, including tens of gigabytes of Indian immigration, flight, and visa records. The same system runs extensive collection of its own citizens’ identifiers through national ID, facial recognition, and social-credit infrastructure.

Those two source countries supply the large majority of H-1B petitions and renewals. The same system that brings the workers also places many of them inside companies that hold government mail, health records, financial data, and critical infrastructure. 

Screening is a weak paper exercise Background checks, as well, nobody is conducting onsite interviews. 

It sure is a good thing the two largest source countries for the program that puts foreign engineers next to American systems are so carefully screened that identity theft and data exposure stay over there, and that sensitive U.S. information is never offshored into those environments.

Otherwise, every day we would be hearing of an other data breach of our financial, medical, and government data.    

Right?

Question:

How many more times does the same source-country pattern and the same incomplete control have to appear before the default path for government and critical systems stops treating the screening paperwork as the actual barrier?

Sources
- Statista 2022 survey of identity-theft victims by country
- TransUnion H1 2026 Top Fraud Trends Report (India 7.1 percent suspected digital fraud rate)
- Sophos State of Identity Security 2026
- Resecurity and related reporting on dark-web Aadhaar listings
- Washington Post / New York Times reporting on iSoon / KnownSec leaked files containing Indian immigration data
- UIDAI statements and Indian police cases on Aadhaar/PAN misuse
- Economic Times and Enforcement Directorate reporting on Chinese nationals and illegal instant loan apps in India (Rs 28,000 crore in traced proceeds)
- Prior public reporting and Cyber Safety Review Board findings on Microsoft incidents involving foreign engineers and government systems
- USCIS and DOL data on H-1B source-country distribution

text:
Gregg Roman, The Washington Examiner
Israel has spent three years winning on the battlefield. Since Oct. 7, 2023, it has struck its enemies in seven arenas and restored its standing as the regional power. It has not yet won where wars are finally decided: in the minds of the enemy.
That is the argument of Meir Ben-Shabbat, who headed Israel’s National Security Council from 2017 to 2021, in a new paper, “Shattering the Palestinians’ Hope of Defeating Israel,” released on Oct. 19. Before that, he served some three decades in the Shin Bet, Israel’s counterintelligence service, including as head of the district responsible for Gaza, and he was one of the architects of the Abraham Accords. His conclusion is blunt: achieving Israel’s war aims is necessary but not sufficient. What is missing is the cognitive defeat of the Palestinian national movement, a lasting change in its belief that Israel can be beaten. “Not despair but hope,” he writes, “is what feeds terror and violence.”

For a generation, Israeli and American policy rested on the opposite assumption: that concessions and economic relief would moderate the other side. The Oslo Accords and the 2005 withdrawal from Gaza, Ben-Shabbat argues, taught the Palestinians that pressure extracts concessions. As long as they believe Israel can be defeated, every political process leads back to what he calls an “Oslo 2.”

The Palestinians’ own polling shows how far there is to go. Half told the Palestinian Center for Policy and Survey Research in May 2025 that Hamas’s decision to attack on Oct. 7 was correct, including 59% in the West Bank. In August, 72% said Hamas should not disarm before a full Israeli withdrawal. Support for Hamas has fallen. The belief that Israel can be defeated has not.
Nor has the Palestinian Authority, which some propose to install in Gaza, given anyone reason to think it has changed. It paid terrorists and their families $156 million in 2025, by Israel’s figure. The 1995 Interim Agreement on the West Bank and the Gaza Strip capped its police at 30,000. Its security services now number an estimated 70,000. On Sept. 16, the State Department told Congress that the Palestine Liberation Organization and the PA had “once again” failed to meet their commitments.

That makes this Washington’s decision as much as Jerusalem’s. The United States drafted Security Council Resolution 2803 and leads the Board of Peace that will shape the force and the committee that run Gaza. The resolution holds out a “credible pathway to Palestinian self-determination and statehood” once the PA reforms. PA President Mahmoud Abbas has meanwhile set Palestinian elections for Sept. 11, 2027, and Hamas says it will run within “the largest and broadest possible national coalition.” Americans who remember what the 2006 Palestinian vote produced should not offer an unreformed PA the prize before it has passed the test.

Ben-Shabbat’s policy lines offer an alternative: Disarm Hamas, demilitarize Gaza completely, and keep security control in Israeli hands. Condition reconstruction on disarmament. Keep Turkey and Qatar out of any stabilization force. Do not press for elections that would hand an unchanged PA, and possibly Hamas, a mandate. Document every PA violation and demand its correction.
The government that emerges from Israel’s Tuesday election will inherit these choices, and with them the familiar pressure to trade them for a quiet that does not last. Washington should help it end the Palestinian hope of outlasting Israel, not renew it.

text:
I didn't have any intention to comment on the midterms, American politics, or elections. I still try to exercise that restraint, having learned, through a long and painful process, how little room there is for my voice or for the insights I offer, at this time. I also have other priorities that deserve my attention.

But returning to some foundational, US-focused literature on social capital and civic engagement has reminded me how much I have always cared and continue to care about American public life. And maybe there is a little sadness I continue to feel, like many other Americans, from everything that has happened in America. 

I remain excited about the possibility of a society in which we can engage across differences, tolerate disagreement, and allow our convictions to be challenged without treating every criticism or passionate conviction as betrayal from someone who thinks differently.

I wish our political communities made more room for that, instead of expecting and demanding the kind of loyalty that makes accountability nearly impossible.

And perhaps that is why I find American electoral politics so unbelievably and increasingly frustrating. Within this two-party system, we keep swinging like a pendulum, with each party’s failures becoming the other’s opportunity for rehabilitation. Every election becomes another argument about who is more dangerous, more cruel, more morally indefensible. The pressure to defeat one party becomes a reason to suspend accountability for the other.

What happens to political memory in that process? What happens to the people whose lives were destroyed by policies we are now being asked to move past?

In 2024, many of us asked why genocide was not a red line for liberal Democrats. We did not receive an adequate answer. We were given electoral miscalculations, warnings about “inflammatory” speech, lectures about the importance of “polite decorum,” and demands to be pragmatic, while thousands of children were being mercilessly slaughtered with weapons paid for by our tax dollars.

The question was about the Palestinian fundamental human right to life, and about what obligations follow when the party you support helps sustain the conditions of mass death.

A change in who holds power does not settle that question. Nor does it erase the decisions Democrats made when they held power themselves.

It saddens me to think that the Democratic Party’s reputation can recover after 2024 just because Republicans offer a more openly brutal expression of American power.

Where does that leave accountability for Gaza? What becomes of the choices Democratic leaders made, the support they continued to provide, and the leverage they could have used? Palestinian lives, and the lives of all indigenous and oppressed people, cannot matter only when defending them is compatible with opposing the party in office.

We have reason to worry about the role progressive figures such as El-Sayed and Mamdani can play in this rehabilitation of the Democratic Party, even when their own convictions and policy preferences diverge from those of the party’s leadership. 

People think that Obama was helping El-Sayed when campaigning for him. That may be true. But in the long-run, it was El-Sayed that was helping Obama, in the attempt to control the narrative of his legacy. The "cool handshake" between Obama and El-Sayed on the campaign trail, between a black and brown man, demonstrates a legacy of tokenistic and performative representation. I really hope that people caught that.

The Progressive presence can give people reasons to hope. But that hope can also restore legitimacy to a party whose senior leaders should be investigated and prosecuted for complicity in genocide at the Hague. Admiration for individual progressives in the Democratic Party cannot resolve that larger question.

I noted this concern in an earlier post... but are we honestly going to absorb Gaza into the same political amnesia that has allowed those responsible for Iraq to retain their authority, reputation, and respectability?

How many times can the demands for accountability be deferred by liberal Americans that should care about democracy until they just disappear?

Isn't accountability a necessary component for a sustainable democracy?

I have reflected a great deal on what it means to remain civically engaged when the available political choices leave you so utterly confused, dismayed, disempowered, and even feeling disenfranchised or marginalized when both parties don't represent your views. 

I have been concerned about the erosion of tolerance and civil discourse, as I know many others have. I have also experienced it firsthand, sharing my views with perhaps too much faith that legal protections for freedom of expression, speech, and political orientation would be reflected in a willingness to hear different opinions, especially in academic and policy spaces... all the while watching people leave my life simply because they disagree with me. 

I am shaking my head as I write this, reflecting on the past ten years, because it still boggles my mind that people who value intellectual inquiry can have so little capacity to tolerate disagreement, let alone appreciate what they might learn from it. Yet I am reminded that there is much in the literature on social capital that can help explain this tendency in America and offer some perspective on why we shouldn't take it personally, even when it's all personal.

We should be able to disagree, organize, persuade, and work together. But that requires room to challenge our own political communities, including when doing so is inconvenient for an election. It requires taking people’s moral objections seriously and not treating them as failures of political sophistication.

My attention may be on global politics, but I am also an American, born and raised in Wisconsin, what I like to call the heart of America. I am also someone who has studied American government in advanced levels and participated in the political process. And now I am designing an American government course that I hope I have the opportunity to teach one day.

As a public policy scholar, I am allowed to hold and express my political opinions without being subjected to social or professional repercussions for exercising my freedom of expression. As an American, I also believe I have a responsibility to question what is done with our public resources and in our name, both here in the United States and around the world. The people affected by American power often have no vote in our elections, yet they live with consequences that extend far beyond our electoral cycles.

It is important to reflect on what our claims about democracy mean to people whose suffering we continue to overlook. As Americans, we have every right to expect more from our political life, even when our convictions do not fit neatly within the political system. We should be able to demand accountability from those we elect without being told that our moral convictions are an electoral inconvenience.

Our civic life should also make more room for the voices of those who have had to endure the consequences of our policy decisions. And when the next election comes around, we should remember what we owe them, instead of allowing electoral politics to absolve us of our complicity...

Thanks for reading this post.

text:
$GOOG $MSFT earnings and their guidance for the AI Capex : 

- Demand is Real
- The Machines Now Cost More Than the Money

On Wednesday Alphabet said Google Cloud's revenue had doubled in a year, to $30.7 billion. Its shares still fell almost 10 percent after hours. In the September quarter, the internet's greatest cash machine spent $9.1 billion more than it took in.

That number, more than any growth rate, is the news from the October 28 reports. Alphabet's capital spending reached $51.4 billion, 114 percent more than a year earlier. It now consumes 40 percent of revenue, against 23 percent a year ago, and operating cash flow of $42.3 billion no longer covers it. Microsoft spent $45.2 billion, close to half its revenue. It still produced $18.6 billion of free cash flow, but that was 27 percent less than a year before.

For three years the comforting difference between this boom and the busts of the past was who paid for it. Not fragile upstarts borrowing against hope, but the richest companies in history spending their profits. These results show that difference narrowing. The AI build-out is beginning to be financed like every great infrastructure mania before it, with one difference that makes it riskier rather than safer.

Start with the money. Alphabet's long-term debt stood at $125.1 billion at the end of September, up from $21.6 billion a year earlier. In June it priced $84.75 billion of new equity, including a $10 billion private placement from Berkshire Hathaway and preferred shares paying 6.25 percent. It kept its 2026 capex guidance at $195 billion to $205 billion and said only that 2027 spending would rise significantly. It is doing this as the 10-year Treasury yield climbs back above 5 percent.

It would be easy to read all this as the sound of a bubble. The demand figures argue against that. Azure grew 48 percent, and Microsoft guided to 49 to 50 percent next quarter. Google Cloud's operating margin rose to 36.2 percent from 23.7 percent a year earlier. Microsoft's commercial remaining performance obligation reached $677 billion, up 73 percent, and Google Cloud's backlog hit $561 billion. Together that is about $1.24 trillion of contracted work.

Most telling of all, both companies spent less than analysts had modelled, and not out of caution. Microsoft now expects about $170 billion of capex in calendar 2026, below the roughly $175 billion it pointed to in July, because third-party capacity arrived late. Its finance chief put it plainly: "Customer demand continues to exceed available supply." The constraint is concrete, power and chips, not appetite.

So the demand is real. The harder question is what history says about building ahead of it. 

In June 2002 economists at the FDIC estimated that only 2 to 5 percent of America's fibre-optic cable was actually lit. Telecom firms accounted for 25.8 percent of corporate bond defaults by dollar volume in 2001. Yet the glass outlived its owners. Laying cable cost about 5 percent of what it cost to light it, and later buyers inherited the expensive part almost free.

Britain's railway mania ended the same way. Parliament passed 263 railway acts in 1846. Projects authorised between 1844 and 1846 produced 6,220 miles of track, more than half the length of today's network, even though a third of the authorised lines were never built and many middle-class savers were ruined. The standard consolation of manias is that investors lose and society keeps the tracks.

That consolation fits this boom badly. About three-quarters of Microsoft's quarterly capex went to what the company itself calls short-lived assets, chiefly CPUs and GPUs. These are not rails that run for a century or glass that can wait a decade for traffic. The accounting bill has barely begun to arrive. Alphabet's depreciation rose 49 percent to $8.4 billion in the quarter, while it spent six times that amount on new assets. If demand stumbles, there will be no dark fibre waiting patiently in the ground, only expensive processors growing old.

Then there is the question of who stands on the other side of those backlogs. Google Cloud's chief described extraordinary demand from AI labs. Anthropic's IPO filing shows at least $389.9 billion of compute commitments to Amazon, Alphabet, SpaceXAI and Microsoft, including at least $44.9 billion with Microsoft through May 2033. Its revenue in the first half of this year was $16.28 billion. Much of that revenue, the filing warns, comes from customers who can cut or end their usage with little notice. The hyperscalers' backlogs rest on the labs' commitments, and the labs' commitments rest on consumption that can walk away.

Alphabet's own earnings show how tightly the circle is drawn. It is both supplier and shareholder. A paper loss of $8.7 billion on its equity holdings, after large gains tied to stakes in SpaceX and Anthropic the previous quarter, cut 55 cents from earnings per share. When the customers' valuations move, the landlord's profits move with them.

Someone is already paying. Microsoft has offered buyouts to roughly 60,000 employees, about 27 percent of its workforce. Alphabet's shareholders own a company that has issued tens of billions of dollars in new stock to fund servers. The machines are not simply being bought with spare cash any more. They are being bought with payroll, dilution and debt.

None of this proves the build is a mistake. A cloud business growing 48 percent and another growing 103 percent are not describing a glut. But the question these results raise is no longer whether Big Tech will keep spending. It is on what terms: borrowed money at 5 percent, assets that age in years rather than decades, sold to customers whose own revenue is provisional. The railways and the fibre were forgiven by time. The chips will not get nearly as much of it.

text:
MacBook Pro with Touchscreen, Dynamic Island Announced, Glowing Apple Logo is Back Too!

Key Highlights:
·  The new MacBook Pros finally get touchscreen functionality, with Tandem OLED panels.
·  The notch is gone and replaced by a Dynamic Island.
·  It also brings back the glowing Apple logo.
·  The new MacBooks are available with M5 Pro and M5 Max chip options, up to 128GB unified memory and up to 16TB maxed-out storage.
·  The 14-inch MacBook Pro starts at $2,899, whereas the 16-inch one starts at $3,399.

Big day for @Apple fans!! At the “Pro and Tell” event in Los Angeles, Apple announced its all-new 14-inch and 16-inch MacBook Pros. But this is not the usual refresh; for the first time, the MacBook gets full touchscreen functionality. These new MacBook Pros are also lighter, come with a Dynamic Island, and bring back the nostalgia – a glowing Apple logo.

Here’s what’s new, my thoughts and everything else you need to know about the new MacBook Pros!

Tandem OLED Touchscreen Display

Back in 2010, Steve Jobs rejected the idea of adding touchscreens on the Mac, arguing that reaching up to tap a vertical display causes severe arm fatigue. Apple’s closest experiment with touch on the MacBook was the Touch Bar, introduced in 2016 and then discontinued in 2023.

Fast forward to 2026, the new MacBook Pros finally get touchscreen functionality, something that has existed on Windows-powered laptops for over a decade. One of the reasons to introduce it now could be the fact that the tech is now mature, the hinge is more robust, and there are new use cases beyond simply tapping to open/close an app.

Touch capabilities on the Mac will allow users to interact with the content, play musical instruments on screen, and even manipulate 3D models.

Touch capabilities on the Mac for the first time, opening up a whole new dimension for pros to interact with their content, from manipulating 3D models to playing musical instruments onscreen. Users can also scroll through webpages, pinch to zoom on photos, and much more.

It’s a tandem OLED panel; Apple calls it “PROLED XDR”, which can deliver true-to-life colours, deep blacks, and good brightness and contrast. The screen offers an adaptive 120Hz refresh rate as well. For better efficiency, the refresh rate can drop down to as low as 10Hz based on the on-screen content. What’s more, the screen can deliver up to 2,000 nits of peak brightness.

Dynamic Island comes to MacBook Pro

After introducing the MacBook Pro with a notched display back in 2021, Apple has now done away with it and introduced the Dynamic Island on the new MacBook Pros. The Live Activities, AirDrop Request, Pausing songs and Siri AI that we have already seen on the iPhones, you get all of that on the MacBook Pros too.

Thinner, Lighter Design, and Glowing Apple Logo is Back

The new MacBook Pros are thinner and lighter as well. The 14-inch model is now 230g lighter and weighs just 1.38kg (vs. 1.62kg previous model), and also 0.5mm thinner. Similarly, the 16-inch model is now 320g lighter at just 1.8kg (vs. 2.16kg on the previous model) and 1mm thinner.

My first MacBook was the MacBook Air (2015), and one of the reasons I got that was its thin and light form factor and the glowing Apple logo. The same year, Apple launched the 12-inch MacBook when it removed the glowing logo to make the display lid thinner, and later removed it from Pro lineup in 2016, and from the Air in 2018. In 2021, I upgraded from the MacBook Air to the MacBook Pro M1 Pro, and I always missed the glowing logo. Now seeing the logo back, makes me feel nostalgic.

M5 Pro, M5 Max Power with up to 128GB Unified Memory, 16TB Storage

The new MacBook Pros come with the powerful M5 Pro/M5 Max SoCs, designed for demanding workflows, from musicians and content creators to developers running AI tasks, LLMs with hundreds of billions of parameters, completely on-device.

MacBook Pro 14, 16 with M5 Pro
·  The base MacBook Pro with M5 Pro chip comes with a 15-core CPU and a 16-core GPU, with 24GB of Unified Memory and 1TB storage.
·  It is configurable with up to an 18-Core CPU and a 20-Core GPU.

MacBook Pro 14, 16 with M5 Max
·  For those who want more performance, they can go for the M5 Max chip with an 18-core CPU and a 32-core GPU, which also comes with 36GB of Unified Memory and 2TB of storage.
·  The chip is configurable up to an 18-core CPU with a 40-core GPU, and it gets 48GB of Unified Memory and 2TB of storage.

Unified Memory can be configured to 36GB/48GB/64GB and 128GB, whereas storage options can be configured to 1TB/2TB/4TB/8TB and all the way up to16TB.

In terms of pricing, the 14-inch MacBook Pro starts at $2,899 (INR 349,900), whereas the 16-inch one starts at $3,399 (INR 409,900).

Overall, the new MacBook Pros seem to offer a good package for developers and content creators. One thing it missed, something that I was expecting, is built-in 5G connectivity. But I think we may have to wait another year for it.

text:
Well, this is an interesting thread and worth reading.

Databases have always been mission critical in software. Most people spreadsheets as databases but in the world of software you need relational tables. And if you want semantic search and other superintelligent features, you need the best database product.

Two weeks ago I went to Snowflake World Tour NYC to meet with their sales team, partners and customers. Databases are changing rapidly as superintelligence models become more agentic. I've been using Supabase for years but I need a deeper understanding of what enterprises are doing.

I completely forgot how massive Databricks is as a private company. They might have twice the annual revenue as Snowflake now. Both of these companies were founded in 2012-13.

Snowflake has been a spotlight business for two reasons: 1) they IPO'd near the peak market in Q4 2020. The stock might have been worth more than IBM with a ~100x sales multiple at open; 2) Frank Slootman, the infamous Amp it Up, CEO was running Snowflake.

Databricks has been quite been they have definitely growing faster. I've seen them as customers for more businesses for the past 2-3 years. The Superintelligence wave is working in their favor, and why Ali is recommending the token pass through below. The back and forth by both database CEOs will be worth watching until Databricks goes public.

As an aside, I'll mention a similar experience I had earlier this year shopping for new business software. Before superintelligence went agentic, I had always had a problem updating my CRM.

For years, I tested multiple apps and could never find a good solution. I've gone back and forth between Salesforce, Hubspot, Streak, fintech specific and more. All of them are good within individual niches.

Salesforce is good for outbound. Hubspot is built for inbound. Streak integrates with gmail. etc etc etc.

However, I ran into a serious problem late last year as agents became mainstream. My HubSpot CRM at the time had a restricted API and made it very difficult to access my data warehouse for all my contacts, companies, notes, and emails. It's a very good app. It's very well designed for manual updates. But it was well equipped for agents or MCPs in Q1 2026. The Breeze assistant was terrible.

By January/February, I reached out to Salesforce for some custom solutions. I had used them many years ago, so I already had a relationship within the financial services team. They made a good offer for a couple of product packages. Obviously, it was sold as an annual license, so I paid upfront. However, setting it up, it was well built for outbound because Agent Force is an excellent tool.

Before viewing Dreamforce, I knew Salesforce was best equipped to work with multiple agents because they have best-in-class CRM. HubSpot, in comparison, is designed for marketing-first businesses, so they have better landing pages and inbound forms. What I found was Breeze was better designed to work internally. The HubSpot app and Agentforce were better designed to work externally with clients. When it came to making sales and proposals, Salesforce was a better tool.

Now, this all comes down to preference, but I did find Salesforce to be more agentic-friendly than Hubspot. However, it still had limitations because Salesforce can become very expensive when you want to access the internal database for your own information, and it's hard to change and update data after it's already in Salesforce. The app feels very rigid and Web 1.0.

I ended up making some version of a custom, personalized CRM that's an extension of my Gmail and other communication tools. Now it works well with Grok and Gemini, but it's API-first, built on a database, and can plug into any model. I've seen some new CRMs built that are similar and worth it if you have a team. I think they'll achieve nine-figure valuations and are more modular than Salesforce and HubSpot.

When it comes to choosing a CRM or database, it really comes down to personal preference and how your business is designed. While HubSpot is a very good product for email and marketing, their agent was designed for internal use. Salesforce is better equipped for sales and proposals, so their agent was designed for external use. Looking at the surface, it would be hard to tell the difference, but you have to be a user. It's a technical difference that, once you make the investment, it would be very difficult to reverse if you're a larger corporation with a +25 person sales team.

I think this is the debate that's happening between Databricks and Snowflake right now. Companies that are building custom solutions with superintelligence, agents, and MCPs have to think about the limitations of what their current tech stack is offering. Otherwise, you'll have to pay more and have more plugins, which will result in breakage and increase your maintenance costs. There's no simple solution and no one-size-fits-all, and it might take too much time and money to build your own, so you do need to rely on the best third-party apps. You wont vibe code an enterprise CRM or database anytime soon.

P.S. I'm not sure how Sridhar will respond back to Ali. But I do know if Frank Slootman was running Snowflake, he'd Amp it Up.

Hey buffalo, please don’t sit there telling people you feel sorry for those who have nobody, no family to turn to and no financial help. Some of us actually lived that reality, and we didn’t have the luxury of sitting around feeling sorry for ourselves.
I grew up having to pick myself up, make the best of the cards I was dealt, work hard, make my own choices wherever I could, and build a life for myself without having people come to my rescue. Nobody came to save me. I had to learn to stand on my own two feet, create my own opportunities and make something of my life. And do you know what that taught me big back? Resilience, independence, strength and compassion. It taught me to appreciate what I have, to value the life I’ve built. To be grateful for the little things in life. 
What I find insulting is listening to someone who has parents who repeatedly show up to clean, help move and do things for them, speak about people who have absolutely nobody as though we’re some unfortunate group to be pitied. You have no idea what it takes to navigate life when there is nobody to call, nobody to lend a hand and nobody to pick up the pieces when things fall apart. I don’t want ya fkn pity. I never needed it. I got on with life. I built a life all by myself. 
I’d rather have lived through the hardships that taught me independence, gratitude and compassion than have every opportunity to build a life with help from others and still fail at life. 
Having a support system is a privilege. Not having one doesn’t make someone lesser, helpless or deserving of your fkn pity, u big back bish. Some of us have built beautiful lives from circumstances that would have broken other people.
So please, don’t confuse having nobody to fall back on with having nothing to offer. Some of the strongest people you’ll ever meet are the ones who had to become their own support system.
And I will always be more proud of the person I became through my struggles than I ever would be of a life in which everything was done for me and this is why I do this for free bish, this bish was smart and knew how to make a life for herself, by herself.

The entire settlement appeared to be abandoned.

There were no people waiting for him. No signs of an ordinary evacuation. The settlers had simply vanished.

John White searched the area, hoping to find his daughter, Eleanor, and his granddaughter, Virginia Dare, who had been born on the island and was the first English child born in the Americas.

Then he discovered something strange.

The word CROATOAN had been carved into a wooden post. Another tree reportedly carried the letters CRO.

White believed the message might point toward Croatoan Island, but bad weather and other difficulties prevented him from completing the search.

The only clue left behind offered no clear explanation of what had happened to the missing settlers.

Greetings Dr. @TobyRichardsUEL and @theironclinic, I hope all is progressing well.

When reading Dr. Nicolas Davis’s article about ferritin in the Guardian, I think about absorption (in general and particularly to iron) and regard the text Vegan for Life by Jack Norris, RD, and Virginia Messina, MPH, RD:  

"There are two stages of iron deficiency. In the first, iron stores become depleted and there may be a decrease in hemoglobin levels and mild symptoms like tiredness and difficulty concentrating. In the next stage—overtime iron deficiency anemia—hemoglobin drops to subnormal levels which can cause symptoms such as pale skin, fatigue, weakness, shortness of breath, an inability to maintain body temperature, loss of appetite, and hair loss. But these symptoms can also be due to other nutritional deficiencies or conditions, and true iron-deficiency anemia can be diagnosed only through a blood test...Foods contain two forms of iron, called home and nowhere iron. Heme iron is much more readily absorbed by the body and is not much affected by other factors in diet. Nonheme iron is absorbed at a much lower level, and its absorption can be inhibited or enhanced by other dietary components, including phytate...The effects of vitamin C on iron absorption are rather dramatic. Just 5 ounces of orange juice, providing 75 milligrams of vitamin C, can quadruple the amount of iron you absorb from a meal. In one study in India, children with iron-deficiency anemia (who probably did not have high vitamin C intakes) were given 100 milligrams of vitamin C at lunch and dinner for sixt days. Most made a full recovery with a significant improvement in their anemia. But simply taking a daily vitamin C supplement won't improve your iron status, since the iron and vitamin C must be consumed at the same time...You should know, however, that certain dietary factors like tannins in coffee and tea and high doses of calcium reduce absorption of nonheme iron. It's important to take calcium supplements between meals, and if you are trying to maximize iron absorption, to avoid drinking coffee and tea with meals." (pp. 108–110)

Nutrition requires a savoir faire, if one will, so one may healthfully regard oneself well. I think absorption is a critical factor to observe, especially considering how timing and pairing of ingredients may effect effectiveness of consumption, nutrition-wise. Oh, parameters of health are quite fascinating! What healthful progression(s) might the future hold via research and development regarding health? (It is important to note the text offers other methods to boost iron absoprtion.)

Onward and Upward,
Kevin Dufresne

Reference
Norris, J., & Messina, V. (2020). Vegan for Life.

text:
Sri Lankan Tamils and Tamil Nadu Tamils: A Shared Language, Two Histories, and a Living Cultural Connection
The Tamil people of Sri Lanka and Tamil Nadu share one of the oldest and richest linguistic and literary traditions in South Asia. Connected by the narrow Palk Strait, these communities have maintained relationships through trade, migration, religion, literature, music and family connections for centuries. Yet, despite their shared language and cultural heritage, Sri Lankan Tamils and Tamil Nadu Tamils have developed distinct historical experiences, regional identities and political traditions.
Understanding their relationship requires looking beyond similarities and differences. It is a story of an ancient language that connects millions of people across national borders, while showing how geography, colonialism and modern political developments have shaped two related but distinct societies.
The history of these communities is not a story of one group being more authentically Tamil than the other. Both are part of the wider Tamil-speaking world, with their own contributions to its cultural heritage.
Ancient Connections Across the Palk Strait
The Palk Strait separates northern Sri Lanka from the southeastern coast of Tamil Nadu. Although it forms an international maritime boundary today, the waters between the island and the Indian mainland have connected communities for centuries.
Fishing, maritime trade, religious travel and the movement of merchants helped establish lasting relationships between the two regions. People travelled in both directions, bringing goods, skills, religious practices and cultural ideas.
Ancient Tamil literature contains references to Eelam, a historical Tamil name associated with Sri Lanka. Literary works, inscriptions and archaeological evidence help researchers investigate the long history of contact between southern India and the island.
However, these sources must be interpreted carefully. Early references to Tamil-speaking people do not automatically establish the exact boundaries of modern ethnic communities. Identities developed over time through migration, settlement, political organisation and cultural interaction.
The historical connection between Sri Lanka and Tamil Nadu is therefore best understood as a long process rather than a single migration or one founding event.
How Sri Lankan Tamils Developed a Distinct Identity
Sri Lankan Tamils have longstanding historical roots in the island, particularly in the Northern and Eastern Provinces. Their communities developed through centuries of settlement, trade, political change and interaction with other groups.
Northern Sri Lanka became home to important Tamil-speaking settlements and political centres. During the medieval period, the Jaffna Kingdom emerged as a significant regional power, contributing to the development of Tamil political institutions, religious traditions and literary culture.
In the east, Tamil-speaking communities developed their own regional traditions shaped by coastal settlements, agriculture, fishing, trade and relationships with neighbouring populations.
Over generations, these experiences contributed to distinctive Sri Lankan Tamil identities. Local customs, dialects, religious institutions and family traditions evolved within the island's social environment.
Sri Lankan Tamils also include different religious communities. Although Hinduism is prominent, Christianity has a long history among Tamil-speaking communities, particularly in parts of the north and east.
Their identity cannot be reduced to language alone. It reflects the accumulated experiences of generations who have lived, worked and established communities in Sri Lanka.
Tamil Nadu: The Historical Heartland of Tamil Language and Literature
Tamil Nadu occupies a central place in the history of Tamil language, literature and classical cultural traditions.
The region is closely associated with Sangam literature, a celebrated body of early Tamil poetry that provides insight into ancient society, love, warfare, trade, kingship and the natural environment.
Over many centuries, Tamil Nadu developed major literary, religious and artistic traditions. The Chola, Pandya and Pallava dynasties contributed to political history, temple architecture, sculpture, literature and the spread of cultural influences across the Indian Ocean.
Large temple complexes, devotional poetry, classical music and dance traditions became important features of the region's cultural heritage.
Tamil Nadu also experienced major changes under European colonial rule and the later formation of modern India. During the twentieth century, Tamil linguistic identity became particularly influential in regional politics, including movements that opposed the imposition of Hindi and promoted the public use of Tamil.
Today, Tamil Nadu is an Indian state with its own elected government within the Indian constitutional system. Its people participate in a wider Indian national identity while maintaining a strong regional Tamil identity.
This political and historical setting differs significantly from that of Tamil-speaking communities in Sri Lanka.
The Tamil Language: One Language, Many Voices
One of the strongest connections between Sri Lankan Tamils and Tamil Nadu Tamils is their shared language.
Tamil is a classical Dravidian language with an exceptionally long literary tradition. It is used in education, literature, journalism, cinema, religious ceremonies and everyday communication across both regions.
Nevertheless, spoken Tamil is not identical everywhere. Regional dialects reflect different histories, local influences and patterns of social interaction.
In Sri Lanka, Jaffna Tamil is widely recognised for its distinctive pronunciation, vocabulary and grammatical features. Batticaloa Tamil has its own characteristics, while Tamil-speaking communities in the central highlands also maintain distinctive varieties.
Tamil Nadu likewise contains many regional speech varieties, including those associated with Chennai, Madurai, Tirunelveli, Kongu Nadu and other areas.
A person from Jaffna and a person from Chennai may recognise the same basic language while noticing differences in everyday vocabulary, accent and expressions.
These variations are a normal feature of a language spoken across different regions. They do not make one variety more authentic or culturally valuable than another.
Formal written Tamil, education, literature and films provide important common ground, helping speakers from different places communicate despite differences in everyday speech.
Religious Traditions and Shared Devotion
Religion forms another important connection between Sri Lankan Tamils and Tamil Nadu Tamils.
Hindu traditions dedicated to deities such as Shiva, Murugan, Vishnu and Amman are influential in both regions. Temple festivals, devotional songs, pilgrimage, family rituals and religious literature preserve traditions that have developed over many centuries.
The relationship between Tamil Nadu and Sri Lankan Hinduism can be seen in shared devotional traditions and the movement of pilgrims, religious teachers and cultural practices across the Palk Strait.
Murugan worship, in particular, has a prominent place in Tamil religious life. Sacred sites in Tamil Nadu and Sri Lanka attract devotees and reflect a wider religious landscape that crosses modern national boundaries.
Christianity also forms an important part of Sri Lankan Tamil heritage. Historic churches in Jaffna and the eastern regions reflect centuries of religious development, including the influence of Portuguese and later European missionary activity.
Tamil Nadu has long-established Catholic and Protestant communities as well.
Religious identity, however, varies between individuals and communities. Shared language does not mean that all Tamils follow the same religion or practise their faith in identical ways.
Food, Family Traditions and Everyday Culture
Food offers a particularly visible example of the relationship between Sri Lankan Tamil and Tamil Nadu cultures.
Rice, lentils, vegetables, coconut, spices and seafood feature prominently in many traditional meals. Idli, dosa, sambar and various forms of rice-based dishes are familiar in both regions, although ingredients and preparation methods differ.
Northern Sri Lankan cuisine is known for distinctive preparations using seafood, crab, prawns, coconut and locally available vegetables. Jaffna also has a reputation for intensely spiced curries and regional dishes associated with family celebrations.
Tamil Nadu cuisine is equally diverse, with substantial differences between coastal areas, inland districts and urban centres.
Religious festivals and family occasions provide further connections. Pongal celebrates the harvest and has deep cultural significance among Tamils in both Sri Lanka and India. Tamil New Year, weddings, naming ceremonies and temple festivals also preserve customs that link generations.
At the same time, each region has developed its own combinations of ingredients, rituals, clothing traditions and social practices.
Cultural similarity should therefore be understood as a shared foundation enriched by local diversity.
Music, Cinema and Literary Influence
Modern media has strengthened connections between Tamil-speaking communities.
Tamil cinema from Tamil Nadu reaches audiences in Sri Lanka and across the global Tamil diaspora. Film songs, actors, dialogue and popular expressions have become familiar to many Sri Lankan Tamil households.
At the same time, Sri Lankan Tamil writers, musicians, journalists and artists have contributed their own distinctive voices to Tamil cultural life.
The literary relationship between the regions also extends far beyond modern cinema. Classical poetry, devotional literature, historical writing and contemporary fiction circulate across geographical boundaries.
Tamil publishing and cultural organisations have helped sustain a shared literary sphere, while local writers continue to explore the particular experiences of their own communities.
These connections demonstrate that cultural exchange is not limited to the movement of people. Books, music, films and digital media allow ideas to travel between regions and across generations.
Colonialism and the Different Paths of History
Although Sri Lankan Tamils and Tamil Nadu Tamils share ancient cultural connections, colonialism shaped their modern histories in different ways.
Tamil Nadu came under British colonial administration as part of British India. Its later political development was influenced by Indian nationalism, regional linguistic movements and the establishment of the Republic of India in 1950.
Sri Lanka, then known as Ceylon, experienced Portuguese, Dutch and British rule before gaining independence in 1948. Following independence, debates over language, citizenship, political representation and national identity became central to relations between the country's communities.
The introduction of Sinhala as the sole official language under the 1956 Official Language Act became a major source of Tamil grievance. Subsequent political tensions, violence and the civil war profoundly affected Sri Lankan Tamil society.
These developments influenced migration, education, employment, political organisation and the relationship between Sri Lankan Tamils and their counterparts in India.
Tamil Nadu's regional language politics followed a different trajectory within India's democratic and federal framework. The two communities therefore developed distinct modern political experiences despite their linguistic and cultural connections.
Understanding these differences is essential to explaining why shared Tamil identity does not automatically produce identical political aspirations.
An Important Distinction: Sri Lankan Tamils and Up-Country Tamils
The Tamil-speaking population of Sri Lanka is itself diverse.
Sri Lankan Tamils, often associated historically with the north and east, have a different historical background from Up-Country Tamils, also known as Malaiyaha Tamils.
Many ancestors of the Up-Country Tamil community migrated from southern India during British colonial rule, particularly in the nineteenth and early twentieth centuries, to work on plantations in Sri Lanka's central highlands.
Over generations, this community developed its own social institutions, political movements and cultural traditions within Sri Lanka.
Although Up-Country Tamils share historical and linguistic connections with Tamil Nadu, they also have a distinct identity shaped by plantation labour, citizenship struggles and their long experience of life in the island.
It is therefore important not to treat all Sri Lankan Tamils as one historically identical group. Their experiences differ according to region, religion, occupation and family history.
Migration, Family Connections and the Tamil Diaspora
The relationship between Sri Lankan Tamils and Tamil Nadu Tamils has continued through migration.
Geographical proximity has made Tamil Nadu an important destination for Sri Lankans seeking family connections, education, employment or refuge. During Sri Lanka's civil war, many Tamil civilians crossed the Palk Strait to escape violence and insecurity.
Others migrated to countries such as Canada, the United Kingdom, France, Australia and Germany, creating large Tamil diaspora communities.
These movements have strengthened connections between people living in Sri Lanka, India and overseas. Family networks, cultural associations, religious institutions and digital communication allow people to maintain relationships across borders.
Yet migration has also created different experiences of belonging. For some, identity is closely connected to ancestral villages and family histories; for others, it is shaped by life in a new country and relationships with multiple cultures.
The modern Tamil world is consequently both regionally rooted and internationally connected.
Two Political Identities, One Wider Cultural Heritage
Sri Lankan Tamils and Tamil Nadu Tamils share a strong linguistic and cultural relationship, but they belong to different political communities.
Sri Lankan Tamils are citizens and residents of Sri Lanka, where their history is connected to the island's political institutions, regional traditions and relationships with other communities.
Tamil Nadu Tamils participate in the political life of India while maintaining a distinctive regional identity centred on Tamil language and culture.
These identities can coexist with a broader sense of Tamil cultural belonging. A person may feel connected to Tamil literature, music and religious traditions across the world while also identifying strongly with Sri Lanka, India or another country.
Shared ancestry or language does not require identical political opinions, and neither community speaks with a single voice.
Respecting these differences makes it possible to recognise cultural kinship without overlooking the historical experiences of each society.
The Enduring Connection Between Sri Lanka and Tamil Nadu
The story of Sri Lankan Tamils and Tamil Nadu Tamils is a story of connection and distinction.
Their shared language, literary heritage, religious traditions, food and family customs reflect centuries of contact across the Palk Strait. Their differences reveal how separate political histories, regional environments and social experiences have shaped the communities over time.
Neither community needs to be measured against the other to establish its place within Tamil history. Tamil Nadu has made extraordinary contributions to classical Tamil literature and cultural traditions, while Sri Lankan Tamils have developed their own rich heritage through centuries of settlement, regional kingdoms, religious institutions and literary achievement.
Together, these communities form important parts of a wider Tamil-speaking world that extends far beyond the boundaries of India and Sri Lanka.
Preserving this heritage requires historical research, language education, cultural exchange and respect for regional diversity. It also requires recognising that shared culture can build understanding without erasing differences.
Across the Palk Strait, the connection between Sri Lanka and Tamil Nadu remains a powerful reminder that languages and cultures can unite people across borders while allowing each community to retain its own history and identity.

text:
Part 7 

These were not all expressions of one conspiracy. They were different forms of power that sometimes intersected. Their common feature was the separation between public explanations and the mechanisms through which decisions were actually made.

Malcolm believed that people subjected to these systems had to understand them before they could change them.

This is where his intellectual legacy begins to converge with the later years of Martin Luther King Jr.

King increasingly challenged the relationship between racial injustice, poverty, and American military policy. In April 1967, at Riverside Church in New York, he delivered Beyond Vietnam, a speech criticizing the war and examining the moral consequences of American intervention abroad. He was also developing the Poor People’s Campaign, which sought to address economic insecurity across racial lines. King was assassinated in Memphis on April 4, 1968, while supporting striking sanitation workers.

Malcolm and King differed profoundly over nonviolence, political strategy, and the role of interracial alliances. Those differences should not be erased. But in their final years both were examining how political inequality was sustained by economic arrangements and institutional decisions that extended beyond the immediate question of segregation.

The resemblance is intellectually significant. It does not establish that the same people organized their murders.

The assassination of John F. Kennedy in November 1963 raises a separate historical problem. Kennedy’s government was involved in major conflicts over Cold War strategy, intelligence activity, Cuba, civil rights, and foreign policy. A congressional investigation later concluded that his death probably resulted from a conspiracy, although its findings and supporting evidence remain disputed. The government and institutional conflicts of his presidency offer legitimate areas of historical research, but a demonstrated connection between his assassination and Malcolm X’s murder has not emerged from the evidence considered here.

The killing of Charlie Kirk in September 2025 is more recent still. Like other politically prominent figures, he became the subject of intense public disagreement before his death. The criminal proceedings must establish responsibility in that case on their own evidence. It would be irresponsible to impose upon it conclusions derived from Malcolm, King, or Kennedy merely because the deaths occurred within politically charged circumstances.

Nevertheless, the comparison raises a difficult question worth preserving. When a prominent public figure is murdered, how do investigators distinguish between the grievances of the immediate perpetrator, the influence of organizations or ideological environments, and the possible involvement of people who never approached the victim?

The answer cannot be found in a person’s notoriety, the number of powerful enemies he accumulated, or the convenience of his death to others. It must be reconstructed through records of decisions and actions: communications, financial transfers, relationships, physical movements, forensic evidence, witness testimony, and subsequent attempts to obstruct an investigation.

Malcolm X would have recognized the importance of examining these relationships. His speeches repeatedly challenged people to look beyond visible authority and investigate the institutions responsible for political outcomes. But intellectual fidelity to Malcolm does not mean turning every unexplained event into a single theory of hidden coordination. It means examining power rigorously enough to distinguish responsibility that can be demonstrated from suspicion that remains unresolved.

It was black and white T.V., that's what my mother's sister could afford to give my sweet Grannie Smith. Once in a while the family would be at her little apartment in Denver and watch this man, Billy Graham, and hope that the man who was also part of his show, Georgia Beverly Shea, might sing "How Great Thou Art".

When my mother was a little girl in Alabama she drank lye that was being used to make soap.  Grannie prayed and told the Lord that if he would let her daughter live she would devote her life to him. 

Part of that devotion was to teach the grandchildren the Old and New Testaments. We memorized scriptures in the New Testament. We knew all the books of the Bible. We went to church we even went to Youth For Christ at the Phipps auditorium.

text:
Franz Kafka begged his best friend to burn everything he ever wrote.

The friend said no.

Thank god, because 100 years ago Kafka described the exact world you woke up in today.

He wasn't a philosopher. He was an insurance clerk in Prague who wrote at night. But he saw four things coming that most of us still haven't named.

1. Systems with no face.
In The Trial, a man is arrested and never told why. Nobody is cruel to him. Everyone just follows procedure.
That's the trap: when everyone is "just doing their job," nobody is responsible.
Sound like the last time you tried to reach a human at customer support?

2. The door that was only yours.
In "Before the Law," a man waits his whole life at a gate for permission to enter. As he dies, the guard tells him the door was meant only for him, and now it's closing.
How many of us are still waiting for permission nobody was ever going to give?

3. Your worth equals your output.
In The Metamorphosis, Gregor wakes up as an insect. His family's first panic isn't about him. It's about who will pay the bills now.
The moment he stops being useful, he stops being seen as a person.
Read that again in the age of productivity metrics.

4. Hope that isn't ours.
Kafka reportedly said there is "an infinite amount of hope, but not for us."
Not despair. Just brutal honesty.

Kafka never offered answers. He said a book must be "the axe for the frozen sea within us." He wasn't writing to comfort us. He was writing to wake us up.

Now look around.

Accounts locked by systems with no human to ask.
Algorithms deciding without giving a reason.
People ranked by their output.

This is Kafka's world, with a nicer interface.

The way out is still the most human thing there is: someone who listens, explains, and takes responsibility.

In an age of systems, be the person in the room.

text:
#HarryPotter #HarryPotterfanfiction

You are Norma Teach. A young, pretty, optimistic but otherwise normal witch professor at Hogwarts. And you LOVE your job! Who wouldn't?

Dumbledore is the hero of the Wizarding World, and he's so amazing and awe inspiring. And he fought You-Know-Who and all and won World War II against his ex-boyfriend (which is kind of weird but whatever!) He's so nice and his eyes twinkle and he's just a big old softie!

And then he decides, out of the blue, to hire a former racist terrorist to be Potions Master! Like, that's literally what he is! He has murdered women and children! For being Muggleborn! He had a creepy obsession with Lily Potter, who his boss murdered!

(And don't tell me nobody knew or speculated, I have been a teacher, it is NOTHING but gossip).

And more than that! This guy is still acting like the Pureblood bigoted terrorist he IS! He's teaching the Slytherins to be utter DICKS to everyone not of Pureblood! Or at least, not stopping them from being dicks because of that! He's turned the Points System into a petty game just to let his House win! When you talk to him about this, he just sneers and insults you and is an utter dick and doesn't seem to realize we're supposed to be teaching kids and NOT acting like them! Because he's still a terrorist dickbag!

So you go to Dumbledore and he offers a lemon drop and you politely say no and then you say "Headmaster! I really respect you, you're amazing and awesome, and I love my job! But why in the hell did you hire a TERRORIST to teach children?! Why is he not in jail?!"

And Dumbledore goes "He's seen the error of his ways."

And you're like "Okay, so, did he turn in a lot of his fellow Death Eaters? Did he save children? Did he invent a potion to fix the after effects of the Crutacious Curse? Something?"

And Dumbledore is like: "Well no... He did actually murder and torture a LOT of people. Like, so many. But he was my spy in Voldemort's camp."

And you're like: "For how long?"

And Dumbledore is like: "He became my spy right after Voldemort was killed."

And you're like: "Are you kidding me?! He became your spy right after the war was OVER and HIS SIDE LOST?!"

Dumbledore is like: "Yeah. Yeah, it worked out pretty nicely. And then I decided to make him a teacher and let him be around children."

And you're like: "WHY?!"

And Dumbledore is like: "Please trust me, everything is fine."

But everything is totally NOT fine. And you keep trying to talk to Dumbledore because you are a good teacher, and you respect Dumbledore, but why, oh why, is he letting this guy do as he pleases?! Potions used to be so much fun! It's such an important subject! You care, man, YOU CARE!

And you see Snape running off to speak with Dumbledore in secret all the time and they keep you out of these meetings and nothing changes! Dumbledore keeps promising things will change but he keeps everyone else out of his plans! Even Minerva McGonnagal, his second in command! You respect this lady so much too! But when you talk to her about the literal baby murdering terrorist teaching at this school, SHE says "Trust Dumbledore!"

And the DADA teacher keeps leaving or dying or being mysteriously replaced by a mannequin that's also a sex doll every year! The whole Defense against the Dark Arts program is a joke! Your colleagues from other nations are laughing at your shitstain of a school, and Hogwarts, oh, Hogwarts used to be wonderful! It used to be tops! But now it's just some sad joke, but maybe, maybe things will get better!

And the years go by and things do not get better, they just get worse! And you really keep trying to care but damnit, isn't Dumbledore supposed to be a schoolteacher? What's the deal? You just want to teach kids and help them grow up into amazing, wonderful adults and show them how amazing magic is! That's your dream!

And then Harry Potter comes along and shit gets REALLY FUCKING CRAZY, man. I mean SO Crazy! Dumbledore makes you make a trap for something! Some kind of giant puzzle, with a door guarded by a Cerberus! IN A SCHOOL FULL OF CHILDREN! Someone sets Snape on fire, and you see it's a student and you realize "This, this was inevitable. It is only surprising it didn't happen sooner. This school should have like ten shooters, the pressure is so high!" You even tell Dumbledore "You've got to do something sir! It's only a matter of time before some kid starts blasting heads off! They'll start with Snape but who knows where it will end?!"

He offers you a lemon sherbert. You sigh and say no thanks.

Finally at the end of the year, it turns out that Dumbledore was hiding the Philosopher's Stone, the ultimate Cheat Code, right in Hogwarts. I mean, it's not surprising that You-Know-Who was after it. It's surprising that You-Know-Who was on the back of a fellow Teacher's head the whole time (That guy was actually nice. Stuttered a lot but you had staff meetings and he even got you all some Danish pastries once.) That guy is dead. Harry Potter, HARRY FUCKING POTTER, murdered him. With his bare hands.

Like, what the hell? How? Why? WHAT?

And he gets awarded points for it! HOUSE POINTS! Just because apparently Snape and Dumbledore have this weird House Cup thing going where Dumbledore let Snape cheat the system blatantly for years but now, Dumbledore is just gonna cheat right back! Right at the last moment! You can see Slytherin students FLINCHING whenever he says "HOWEVER!"

Is this how it ends?! Shouldn't we call the Aurors? Shouldn't Harry get looked over by actual Healers and not just the school nurse? When will Snape get set on fire again?!

You try one last time to talk to Dumbledore about this, like you are basically BEGGING him to make some sense out of all of this. You are SO respectful, you are trying not to think that he's insane or evil, you are really trying.

HE OFFERS YOU A LEMON SHERBERT.

You finally quit. Not your job, no, you can't. The job market for wizard teachers in Britain is awful right now. But you quit trying. Dumbledore's got this incomprehensible game going on involving everyone as a chess piece. Harry Potter is part of it. You don't know the details, you don't think you'll ever know, you're just tired, man. You're tired.

You go and just get some drinks at the Hogshead. Hagrid says "Yeah, an I hatched a dragon this year too!"

"Of course you fucking did," you mutter, before you pound back the hardest stuff you can afford.

Later...

Norma: "Professor McGonnagal, you're my idol! I worked so hard to be just like you! Tell me! How do you deal with all of the Headmaster's madness?!"

McGonnagal: "That's actually very simple, my dear!"

McGonnagal pulls out a bottle of the hardest scotch whiskey known to man, in a never ending bottle, and begins to chug right from it.

She keeps doing this for a few minutes before Norma goes:

"OH. Okay, so that's your actual answer."

"Oh, that's not all," Minerva added.

"Really?"

"I also lie to myself. Every day I wake up and tell myself that everything will be fine. Everything will be sane and make perfect sense. I know it's a lie, but it helps me keep some small scraps of sanity. Any other questions?"

"Is it too late for me to quit?"

"Probably. Would you like your own bottle?"

"Yes please."

Under the proposed Military Hockey Protection Initiative (MHPI), American infantry personnel will receive regulation shoulder pads, elbow guards, shin protectors, padded hockey pants, and reinforced helmets.

Standard ballistic vests will be replaced with NHL-approved chest protectors. Military officials acknowledge that hockey pads have not been certified to stop rifle ammunition but insist that soldiers will enjoy considerably greater protection against boarding penalties, cross-checking, and unexpected encounters with Philadelphia Flyers fans.

The Army's new combat helmet will also include a chin strap, full facial cage, and an optional mouthguard. Soldiers losing teeth in combat will be encouraged to continue fighting unless more than six are missing.

The Marine Corps immediately endorsed the initiative after learning that hockey players frequently engage in fistfights without waiting for authorization from their commanding officers.
