text:
An archive full of people claiming to be the model, and exactly one of them could prove it. Mary Alexander posed for a 1955 Coca-Cola campaign built by Moss Kendrix, then vanished from the company's records for fifty-two years while her picture kept working. When her niece found the old advertisement and called, the archivists assumed another false claim, so Mary faxed them the letter she had kept since college.

The boy carrying the golf bags was small enough that the strap cut into his shoulder. The men he carried them for ran the Coca-Cola Company.

The boy's name was Moss Kendrix, and he was a Black kid working an Atlanta course for tips. That detail reaches us through a single public radio report built with the curator who keeps his papers in Virginia, and it is the closest thing this story has to a beginning.

Years later he wrote to the company whose bags he had carried, out of the blue. It was 1946, and he was offering to sell them fourteen million customers they had never once tried to reach.

For three years he worked the Atlanta office and the New York office at the same time. The historian Brenna Greer, who has been through his files, uses the word hounding.

In the third year the Black press noticed. Ebony ran a piece called "Brown Hucksters" reporting that Coca-Cola was thinking about hiring a Negro marketing specialist, and it printed no name.

He was thirty-one and the best known Black publicity man in Washington. The article was about him, and even the Black press would not say so.

The silence on the other end of those letters was not an oversight. Coca-Cola had been thinking about Black customers for fifty years, and what it had concluded was that they were a hazard.

That conclusion was born at the soda fountain, and in the South the soda fountain was a white room with stools nobody Black was allowed to sit on. When the company went into bottles in 1899, anyone with a nickel could buy one, and that included Black men in a region already telling itself frightening stories about them.

In 1901 the Atlanta Constitution warned that soft drinks containing cocaine could quietly build a habit in Black drinkers. That same year Asa Candler moved on the formula, and by 1903 the cocaine was out and the sugar and the caffeine were up.

White alarm over who could now afford a bottle became one of the pressures on that recipe, working alongside a rising national campaign against the drug itself. The historian Grace Elizabeth Hale, who has followed the line from the segregated counter to the nickel bottle, names both forces pushing at once.

The company's advertising followed the same instinct for the next thirty years. Through the 1920s and 1930s it left Black America out of the frame entirely, and in Black neighborhoods across the South the drink of choice was Nehi grape and Nehi orange, because Nehi had bothered to ask for the business.

The historian Robert Weems has written about what the rest of the market was doing in those years, which was worse than ignoring. Whole product lines carried brand names built directly out of slurs, because companies that considered Black people irrelevant felt free to insult them without cost.

The exclusion at Coca-Cola was quieter and just as complete. There is a television commercial of theirs from the 1950s in which an all white crowd relaxes at a fountain counter while a voice says that smart shoppers everywhere take time to pause and refresh.

Audrey Davis, the curator in Alexandria who keeps the Kendrix collection, has pointed out the obvious thing about that advertisement. It was inviting Black families into a room where they would have been arrested for sitting down.

The company did see Black people in those years. It saw them as porters, loading the trucks.

Davis puts the rest of it flatly. They were not being seen as salesmen.

The boy with the golf bags had grown up in Beaver Slide, one of the west Atlanta neighborhoods that took shape after the 1906 massacre, near Atlanta University. His mother had moved there to be close to her brother, and the uncle became the father figure in the house.

He went to Morehouse, edited the Maroon Tiger, and used a college newspaper to write about lynching and civil rights. Lena Horne had been a childhood friend, and he would still be able to reach her twenty years later.

In 1939 he founded National Negro Newspaper Week, got into Howard's law school, and turned it down for a public relations job with the National Youth Administration in Georgia. He married Dorothy Marie Johnson, a Spelman student, the same year.

Congress killed the NYA in 1943 and the Army took him, posting him to Fort Benning as an assistant public relations officer. He turned the fort's Black chorus into a war bond tour and got Duke Ellington and Billy Eckstine to appear alongside it.

That tour carried him to the Treasury Department in Washington, and from there to the oddest job of his life. He ran the American publicity for the centennial of the Republic of Liberia, put the Liberian president in a room with Harry Truman in 1947, and commissioned the Duke Ellington work that became the Liberian Suite.

None of it was capital. What he had at the end of it was a phone book with Ellington and Pearl Bailey and Joe Louis in it, in a country full of white executives who could not get a single one of those people to return a call.

He turned that phone book into a business in 1948, the Moss Kendrix Organization, in Washington. The first motto he had embossed on the letterhead read, court the Negro market and count the results.

He softened it later into the line he is remembered for, what the public thinks counts. They are the same sentence with the price tag moved.

Coca-Cola put him on retainer in 1951, five years after the first letter, which made him by most accounts the first Black man in America to hold a major corporate account. His proposal opened with a number rather than a plea, stating that fourteen million people made up the Negro market of the United States.

The number was not news to Pepsi, which had gone after those same customers first. Coca-Cola hired Moss Kendrix to catch up.

Catching up started with ice buckets. He drove to Black doctors' conventions and teachers' conferences and dental association meetings, set up a booth, and handed out cold Coca-Cola to people no salesman had ever offered anything to.

His son was with him. Moss Kendrix Jr., who grew up to be an Air Force colonel, remembers being the kid standing behind the booth serving it, and remembers that it was cold.

That is what the job looked like before the famous photographs. A man and a boy and a bucket of ice, in a country where the son's own summary of the situation was that Negroes did not buy Coca-Cola.

Inside the company he went to work on E. Deloney Sledge, the advertising director, a man holding one of the largest advertising budgets on earth. Working with Sledge and the D'Arcy agency, he pulled entertainers and athletes out of his phone book and put them on the page.

In October 1953 a reader turning through Ebony came to a full page in four colors with Goose Tatum of the Harlem Globetrotters and a bottle of Coke. It belonged to Coca-Cola's first real run at Black customers, which had already put Alice Coachman and Jesse Owens on billboards the year before.

Kendrix called it a half measure. Famous faces sold the drink and proved nothing about ordinary Black life, so in 1955 he drove to Clark College and Morehouse looking for people nobody had ever heard of.

At Clark a housemother knocked on a junior's door and told her the company was recruiting Black models. The young woman was Mary Alexander, from Ballplay, Alabama, one of ten children, the second person in her family to reach college.

She had hoed fields in the Alabama heat since she was small. An ice cold Coca-Cola was the treat waiting at the end of those days, and she had her first one at seven or eight years old.

She told the housemother no. The dean asked her again, and she went.

Seventy-five women tried out. She was picked, and she could not understand why, because the other girls were from Atlanta and New York and she thought of herself as a simple country girl.

The first shoot was nerve-wracking, and she walked back to her dorm room afterward and cried a little. Her parents were strict, and she was not sure this was something she should be doing at all.

Coca-Cola paid her six hundred dollars for roughly fifteen advertisements. It covered a full year of her tuition.

What she was hired to do was hold a pose that already existed. The Black models in Kendrix's campaign wore the same clothing and struck the same poses as the professional white models in Coca-Cola's mainstream advertising, and that exact mirroring is Greer's central finding about the work.

The pictures mirrored each other. The circulation did not.

Black advertisements ran through Black magazines and Black newspapers, through storefronts and point of sale placements that were mostly though not only Black, and out on billboards and subway platforms. The two Americas in those photographs almost never shared a page.

That arrangement had a name, and the Supreme Court had struck it down the year before. Greer's reading is that a photograph showing Black and white Americans together would likely have been unpopular in 1955, and so Kendrix built the most exactly separate and exactly equal images in the country.

That same year the NAACP threatened to pull Coca-Cola machines out of its own offices, because a local bottler had said publicly what he thought about segregation. Kendrix went to work quietly to keep those machines where they stood, an episode the historian Jason Chambers documents.

He was himself a member of the NAACP, and of the Urban League, and his obituary would list both. He was also the man Coca-Cola paid to keep the NAACP from embarrassing Coca-Cola.

The thing he pushed hardest for was never the photographs. He kept telling the company to hire Black employees and Black sales representatives, which cost more than a picture and moved a great deal slower.

While he pushed for jobs, the industry he had opened was studying its new market like a specimen. Trade researchers reported that Black households ate thirty percent less cheese than white ones and had a particular fondness for scotch.

In 1962 a trade magazine summed the whole thing up in one sentence, saying the Negro seeks recognition, in commercial affairs as in other areas of life. A people asking for citizenship had been filed under consumer preference.

Chambers names what came out of it that the trade press never saw coming. Once companies understood what Black spending was worth to them, Black spending carried a threat.

Kendrix was selling white executives the same arithmetic organizers already understood. Montgomery walked three hundred and eighty-one days and the bus company lost most of its riders, because Black riders had always been most of the riders.

He kept selling that arithmetic until the work ran out. The Moss Kendrix Organization wound down through the 1970s, while he kept a weekly radio program on WWDC in Washington and served on the board of a Head Start program.

His client list, as his obituary printed it, included F.W. Woolworth. No dates were attached to any of it.

Robert Weems, the historian who catalogued those insulting brand names, drove through his old South Side Chicago neighborhood one day in the 1980s, a place national advertisers had ignored for most of the century. He could not stop counting the billboards.

Cigarettes and malt liquor, block after block, in the neighborhoods that had finally been found. One campaign built around a famous Black actor promised that its product worked every time, and Weems sat with that word, working, and asked what exactly the companies thought was working.

His conclusion about the whole story is harder than any of it. The Black entrepreneurs who taught corporate America to want Black dollars also opened the door for corporations to take the business away from Black owners, and for the liquor and cigarette money to buy influence over Black newspapers and Black organizations.

Kendrix was alive for the first years of those billboards. He died of a heart ailment at his home in Washington on the fourth of January, 1989, at seventy-one.

The Washington Post ran him nine days later, under a headline saying he had owned a marketing firm.

Ten years after that headline, in April 1999, four current and former Black employees sued the Coca-Cola Company over pay, promotions and evaluations. In November 2000 the company settled with roughly two thousand of them for one hundred and ninety-two and a half million dollars, then the largest race discrimination settlement in American history.

Coca-Cola denied the allegations throughout. A settlement is not a finding, and nobody was ever made to say in a verdict what had happened.

Kendrix had sat in that building forty-nine years earlier telling them to hire Black people rather than only photograph them. The argument was still being had, in a federal courtroom, by people who were not born when he made it.

Eighteen years after he died, and fifty-two years after her pictures first ran, Mary Alexander's niece and a high school classmate were going through old photographs and found a face they recognized. They took a picture of the advertisement and called the Coca-Cola consumer hotline.

By the time the message reached the archives, the archivists assumed the claim was false. Jamal Booker, who handles heritage communications for the company, has said they keep a whole file of people claiming to be the models.

Mary Alexander had kept a personal letter from the company from her modeling days. She faxed it in.

Booker's account is that in more than thirty years of people making that claim, she was the only one who ever had proof. Months before the call came, without knowing her name, the company had already selected one of her advertisements for display at the World of Coca-Cola in Atlanta.

They had her face on the wall and nothing to write underneath it. Kendrix had been dead eighteen years, and the only thing left that could close the gap was a piece of paper she had carried out of college and never thrown away.

By then she had been out of that world for half a century. She had gone on to become the first Black teacher at a mostly white Michigan high school, hired after nearly three years of applications and a stretch working as a real estate secretary.

When the principal warned her the students were white, she asked him whether they all had red blood in their veins. He said they did, and she said then she had no problem.

She became a principal at Highland Park High School and later a state director of vocational education in Michigan. She died in September 2024 at ninety, after years of being invited back to Atlanta to tell a story the company had nearly lost.

Nearly lost is exact. Booker said afterward that without a fan of hers, the company would never have known Mary Alexander was out there.

That is the whole margin on this story, one relative going through old photographs. Kendrix's own record runs to more than nine hundred of them, sitting in the Alexandria Black History Museum in Virginia along with the letters and the scripts and the press releases and the clippings.

In 2020 the Virginia Association of Museums named that collection one of the ten most endangered artifacts in the state.

He pulled those students out of Atlanta classrooms and put them in front of the whole country, in golf shirts and tennis skirts and prom dresses, in dungarees playing leapfrog, holding the bottle at the angle they were told to hold it. Many of their names were never preserved beside the pictures.

The pictures are catalogued. Most of the people in them are not.

I put a lot of effort into researching and sharing stories that matter.

She was only 14 years old. The man taking her photograph was a serial k*ller. And the image that captured one of her final moments would later become a crucial piece of evidence in bringing him to justice.

Her name was Regina Kay Walters.

In 1990, Regina and her boyfriend, 18-year-old Ricky Lee Jones, were hitchhiking after leaving their homes in Texas. They accepted a ride from Robert Ben Rhoades, a long-haul truck driver who would become known as the “Truck Stop K*ller.”

It was a decision that changed their lives forever.

Rhoades k*lled Ricky and kept Regina captive. During her captivity, he took photographs of her. One of the most haunting images shows the frightened teenager standing inside an abandoned barn in Illinois, her hands raised defensively toward the camera.

The man behind the camera was the person who would k*ll her.

Regina was strangled, and her body was left in the barn. Her remains were discovered in September 1990, months after Rhoades had been arrested in an unrelated incident involving another young woman he had held captive in his truck.

Investigators later recovered photographs of Regina that helped connect Rhoades to her m*rder. In 1992, he pleaded guilty to her k*lling and received a life sentence.

The photograph remains deeply disturbing—not because Regina should be remembered only through her suffering, but because it offers a glimpse of a child trapped in circumstances no child should ever face.

Behind the image was a 14-year-old girl with a life that should have continued. She deserved safety, the chance to grow up, and the opportunity to decide what her future would look like.

Her story also reminds us of the vulnerability of young people who leave home or travel without a safe place to turn. Their circumstances should never make them less deserving of protection, compassion, or justice.

Regina was not simply a victim in a serial k*ller’s story. She was a daughter, a teenager, and a human being whose life mattered.

May she be remembered for more than the photograph taken by her k*ller—and may her name never be lost behind his.

text:
AI gives learning science a measurable feedback loop

Joe Liemandt on Huberman Lab with Andrew Huberman. Joe Liemandt is a technology entrepreneur and principal of Alpha School. The K, 12 model uses AI and individualized learning to help students master academics in two hours a day, leaving time for projects, businesses, experiments and practical skills.

Liemandt argues that individualized AI lessons can meet students at their current level and help them master missing prerequisites, while human guides support motivation and personal development. He says schools should combine high standards with support, measure students' growth as well as achievement, and make difficult work feel connected to goals students care about. Alpha's model pairs two hours of academics with activities in areas such as sports, entrepreneurship, science and creative projects. Liemandt says the approach can expand through vouchers, public-school partnerships and lower-cost programs, while acknowledging that broader system change will take time.

Minute by minute

1. Access does not guarantee learning (3:12)
Liemandt traces the classroom model to mass schooling's industrial-era roots and says it achieved broad access but not consistent learning. He argues that AI and technology make individualized instruction feasible and says Alpha wants to extend its model to a billion students.

2. Schools need standards and support (10:20)
Liemandt says schools provide socialization, structure and motivation that online materials cannot. Alpha sets high standards alongside support. He says 90-some percent of students report loving school, and between 40 and 60 percent said they would rather attend than go on vacation, depending on the session and workshops.

3. Individualized coaching drives progress (22:24)
Liemandt argues that effective academic support should resemble sports coaching. Direct, individualized instruction aimed at each student, rather than a teacher delivering the same lesson to a whole class. He says homeschooling outcomes vary with families' academic expectations, and that one-to-one instruction can work well but is difficult to scale.

4. AI makes mastery scalable (30:01)
Liemandt cites Bloom's Two Sigma work to argue that individual tutoring paired with mastery can put students near the top 2% of performance. He says Alpha students averaged 121 minutes in learning apps last year and learned more than twice as much as they would in six hours of class plus homework. He also argues that teacher training and policy debates often overlook or contest learning science.

5. AI enables a learning feedback loop (43:35)
Liemandt describes AI as a way to measure learning through students' engagement, answers and later recall, rather than as a chatbot. He favors worked examples, gradually removed scaffolding and spaced repetition. He says Alpha's results led it to add initial mastery for younger students, while older students benefited from worked examples and spaced practice.

6. Fluency frees working memory (52:35)
Liemandt says fluent recall keeps basic facts from consuming limited working-memory capacity, which helps with multistep work. He describes a student who raised her math SAT score from 710 to 790 after relearning multiplication tables, and says gifted students can hit a wall if they rely on mental calculation instead of learning to show their work.

7. Master the foundations first (1:00:14)
Liemandt argues that students should master foundational skills before advancing, using basketball ball-handling and math prerequisites as analogies. He says incoming Alpha students averaged 2.2 grade levels behind on assessments, and that in K, 8 a student can cover a grade level in one subject in 20 to 30 hours if motivated.

8. Measure growth, then motivate (1:08:07)
Liemandt says schools should track learning growth, not only grade-level achievement, and that guides help students overcome beliefs that they cannot succeed. He says Alpha has offered $1,000 to reach the top 1% and $100 for a perfect score on a state test at each grade level, using rewards to prompt students to fill gaps and discover what they can do.

9. Purpose makes hard work worthwhile (1:20:49)
Liemandt says suffering is not inherently useful. Students should get easier instruction where possible and accept difficulty when it serves a goal they care about. He describes Alpha's sports academy as pairing two hours of academics with sports, and says students' odds of earning a Division I scholarship double.

10. Life skills belong in school (1:31:09)
Liemandt says Alpha teaches life skills through projects and age-based activities, from kindergarten lessons in earning, saving, spending, investing and donating to middle-school businesses. He describes Founder School, a high-school entrepreneurship program that promises a million dollars in profit or tuition back.

11. Schools should develop builders (1:47:15)
Liemandt argues schools should shift students from consumption to building, with AI handling customized academic lessons and human guides working on development and motivation. He describes Alpha's student-run music festival, where fifth- and sixth-graders formed bands and raised $25,000 in sponsorships.

12. Projects make science tangible (1:57:54)
Huberman asks about hands-on biology. Liemandt says Alpha is redesigning experiments and using projects such as baking and special-effects chemistry to teach lab skills. He describes students spending hours on projects and voluntarily building software at weekend hackathons, arguing that making things helps students engage.

13. Design for different learners (2:06:07)
Liemandt says Alpha's short, engaging academic blocks can help students with ADHD focus, and argues that the program can address some performance differences. He says schools must design for different customers and budgets, describing sports-focused schools and a gifted program rather than assuming one format suits every student.

14. Access requires multiple routes (2:18:35)
Liemandt says Alpha aims to extend access through vouchers, public-school partnerships and lower-cost programs. He reports that more than 120,000 Texas families expressed interest in the Sports Academy through the voucher portal, while Alpha received a little over 1,000 vouchers. He says MIT's Blueprint Labs will evaluate outcomes. He says broader system change could take 20 years and describes a free learning game intended to reach 500 million children.

The link in the reply plays each point from its second.

text:
This triad emerges directly from a rational observation of the world. And if looking away from all dogmatic statements, from all philosophical or theosophical traditions, in so far as these are clothed in conceptual definitions or formulations, we may ask: How has the human mind always expressed the fact that this triad is present not only in the immediate environment, but in the whole world to which man himself belongs? We must then reply: Man gives the name of Spirit to all that can be known within the horizon of the conscious. He designates as the Son or the Logos that which works in the subconscious and throws up only its waves from down below. And to that which belongs equally to the unknown in Nature, and to the part of our own being which is of one kind with Nature, the name of the Father-Principle has always been given, because it was felt to express the relation of the third principle to the other two.

Besides what has now been said concerning the Spirit, the Son and the Father-Principle, it can be taken for granted that other differentiations we have formerly made, and also the differentiations made in this or that philosophy, have their justifications. But we can say that the most widely accepted idea of this differentiation corresponds with the account of it given here.

Now let us ask: How can we characterise the transition from that which belongs to the Spirit, and so plays directly into the conscious life of the soul, to the subconscious element which belongs to the Son-Principle? We shall best grasp this transition if we realise that into ordinary human consciousness there plays quite distinctly the element we designate as Will, in contrast to the elements of ideations and feeling. If we rightly interpret the Bible saying, ‘The Spirit is willing, but the flesh is weak’, it indicates that everything grasped by consciousness lies in the realm of the Spirit, whereas by ‘the flesh’ is meant everything that lies more in the subconscious. As to the nature of the Will, we need only think of that which plays up from the subconscious and enters into our consciousness only when we form concepts of it. Only when we transform into concepts and ideas the dark impelling forces which are rooted in the elemental part of the soul — only then do they enter the realm of the Spirit; otherwise they remain in the realm of the Son-Principle. And since the Will plays through our feelings into the life of ideas, we see quite clearly the breaking out into the conscious of the waves from the subconscious ocean. In our threefold soul-life we have two elements, ideation and feeling, which belong to conscious life, but feeling descends directly into the realm of the Will, and the nearer we come to the impulses of Will, the further we descend into the subconscious, the dark realms into which we sink completely when consciousness is engulfed in deep, dreamless sleep.

Thus we see that the Will-element, because it descends into the realm of the subconscious, stands towards the individual being of man in a relationship quite different from that of cognition, the realm of the Spirit. And so, when we differentiate between Spirit and Son, we may be impelled to surmise that man's relationship to the Spirit is different from his relationship to the Son. How is this to be understood?

Even in exoteric life it is quite easy to understand. Certainly the realm of cognition has given rise to all kinds of debate, but if people would only come to understand one another concerning the concepts and ideas they formulate for themselves, controversy over questions of cognition would gradually cease. I have often emphasised that we no longer dispute over mathematics, because we have raised mathematics entirely into consciousness. The things we dispute about are those not yet raised into consciousness: we still allow our subconscious impulses, instincts and passions to play into them.

So we see that in the realm of cognition we have to do with something more universally human than anything to be found in the subconscious realm. When we meet another human being and enter into the most varied relationships with him, it is in the realm of conscious spiritual life that understanding should be possible. And a mark of a healthy soul-life is that it will always wish and hope to reach an understanding with the other person concerning things that belong to conscious spiritual life. It will be unhealthy for the soul if that hope is lost.
On the other hand, we must recognise the Will-element, and everything in another person's subconscious, as something which should on no account be intruded upon; it must be regarded as his innermost sanctuary. We need consider only how unpleasant to a healthy soul-life is the feeling that the Will of another man is being put under compulsion. It is not only aesthetically but morally unpleasant to see the conscious soul-life of anyone eliminated by hypnotism or any other powerful means; or to see the Will-power of one person working directly on the Will of another. The only healthy way to gain influence over another person's Will is through Cognition. Cognition should be the means whereby one soul comes to an understanding with another. A person must first translate his wishes into a conceptual form: then they may influence another person's cognition, and they should touch his Will only by this indirect route. Nothing else can be satisfactory in the highest, most ideal sense to a healthy life of soul. Every kind of forcible working of Will upon Will must evoke an unpleasant impression.

In other words, human nature strives, in so far as it is healthy, to develop in the realm of the Spirit the life it has in common with others, and to cherish and respect the realm of the subconscious, in so far as it comes to statement in the human organism, as an inviolable sanctuary that should rest in the personality, the individuality, of each man and should not be approached save through the door of conscious cognition. So at least a modern consciousness, attuned to our epoch, must feel if it is to know itself to be healthy.

In later lectures we shall see whether this was so in all periods of human evolution. What has been said today will help us to think clearly about what is outside us and what is within us, at least for our own period. This leads to the conclusion that fundamentally the realm of the Son — embracing everything that we designate as the Son or Logos — must be awakened in each individual as a quite personal concern; and that the realm of common life, where men may be influenced by one another, is the realm of the Spirit.

We see this expressed in the grandest, most significant way in the New Testament accounts of the attitude of Christ Jesus towards His first disciples and followers. ====================== From all that is told concerning the Christ-Event we can gather that the followers who had hastened to Jesus during his life-time were bewildered when His life ended with the crucifixion; with that form of death which, in the land where the Christ Event took its course, was regarded as the only possible expiration for the greatest crimes. And although this death on the cross did not affect everyone as it did Saul, who later became Paul, and as Saul had concluded that someone who suffered such a death could not be the Messiah, or the Christ — for the crucifixion had made a milder impression on the disciples, one might say — yet it is obvious that the writers of the Gospels wished to give the impression that Christ Jesus, through his subjection to the shameful death on the cross, had forfeited some of the effect He had had on the hearts of those around Him.

But with this account something else is connected. The influence that Christ Jesus had acquired — an influence we must characterise more exactly during these lectures — was restored to Him after the Resurrection. Whatever may be our present thoughts about the Resurrection, we shall have to discuss it here in the light of occult science; and then, if we simply go by the Gospel narratives, one thing will be clear: for those to whom Christ appeared after the Resurrection He had become someone who was present in a quite special way, different entirely from His previous presence.

In speaking on the Gospel of St. John I have already pointed out how impossible it would have been for anyone who knew Jesus not to regognise Him after 3 days, or to confuse Him with someone else, if He had not appeared in an altered form. The Evangelists wish particularly to evoke the impression that the Christ appeared in this altered form. But they also wish to indicate something else. For the Christ to exert influence on human souls, a certain receptivity in those souls was necessary. And this receptivity had to be acted on not merely by an influence from the realm of the Spirit but by the actual sight of the Christ-Being.

If we ask what this signifies, we must realise that when a person stands before us, his effect upon us goes beyond anything we are conscious of. Whenever a human being or other being works upon us, unconscious elements affect our soul-life; they are produced by the other being indirectly through consciousness, but he can produce them only if he stands before us in actuality. What the Christ brought about from person to person after the so-called Resurrection was something that worked up from the unconscious soul-powers of the disciples into their soul-life: an acquaintance with the Son. Hence the differences in the portrayal of the risen Christ; hence, too, the variations in the accounts, showing how the Christ appeared to one or other person, according to the disposition of the person concerned. Here we see the Christ-Being acting on the subconscious part of the souls of the disciples; hence the appearances are quite individual, and we should not complain because they are not uniform.

If, however, the significance of the Christ for the world was to be His bringing to all men something common to all of them, then not only this individual working of the Son had to proceed from the Christ, but the element of Spirit, which can encompass something that belongs to all men, had to be renewed by Him. This is indicated by the statement, that after the Christ had worked upon the Logos-nature of man, He sent forth the Spirit in the form of the renewed or ‘holy, Spirit’. Thus was created that element common to all men which is characterised when we are told that the disciples, after they had received the Spirit, began to speak in the most diverse tongues. Here we are shown how the common element resides in the outpouring of the Holy Spirit. And something else is indicated; how different is this out-pouring of the Spirit from the simple imparting of the power of the Son, for in the Acts of the Apostles we are told that certain persons to whom the apostles came had already received the Jesus-baptism, and yet they had now to receive for the first time the Spirit, symbolically indicated by the laying on of hands. In the characterisation of the Christ-working, which acts upon the subconscious impulses of the soul and so must have a personal, inward character, and the Spirit-element, which represents something common to all mankind.

It is this Spirit-element that those who have named themselves ‘Rosicrucians’ have sought to preserve most carefully, as far as human weakness permits. The Rosicrucians have always wished to adhere strictly to the rule that even in the highest regions of Initiation nothing must be worked upon except the Spirit-element which, as common between man and man, is available in the evolution of humanity. It was never an Initiation of the Will, for the Will of man was to be respected as a sanctuary in the innermost part of the soul. Hence the individual was led to those Initiations which were to take him beyond the stage of Imagination, Inspiration, and Intuition, but always so that he could recognise within himself the response which the development of the Spirit-element was to call forth. No influence was to be exerted on the Will.

We must not mistake this attitude for one of indifference towards the Will. The point is that by excluding all direct working upon the Will, the purest spiritual influence was imparted indirectly through the Spirit. When we come to an understanding with another man with regard to entering on the path of knowledge of the Spirit, light and warmth are radiated from the spiritual path, and they then enkindle the Will, but always by the indirect path through the Spirit — never otherwise.

In Rosicrucianism, therefore, we can observe in the highest sense that impulse of Christianity which finds twofold statement: on the one hand in the Son-element, in the Christ-working which goes down deeply into the subconscious; on the other, in the Spirit-working which embraces all that falls within the horizon of our consciousness. We must indeed bear the Christ in our Will; but the way in which man should come to an understanding with each other in life concerning the Christ can be found only — in the Rosicrucian sense — through a conscious soul-life which penetrates ever more deeply into the occult.

In reaction against many other spiritual streams in Europe, the opposite way was taken by those who are usually called Jesuits. The radical, fundamental difference between what we justifiably call the Christian way of the Spirit and the Jesuit way of the Spirit, which gives a one-sided exaggeration to the Jesus-Principle, is that the intention of the Jesuit way is to work directly, at all times upon the Will. The difference is clearly shown in the method by which the pupil of Jesuitism is educated. Jesuitism is not to be taken lightly, or merely exoterically, but also esoterically, for it is rooted in esotericism. It is not, however, rooted in the spiritual life that is poured out through the symbol of Pentacost, but it seeks to root itself directly in the Jesus-element of the Son, which means in the Will; and thereby it exaggerates the Jesus-element of the Will.

This will be seen when we now enquire into the esoteric part of Jesuitism, its various spiritual exercises. How were these exercises arranged? The essential point is that every single pupil of Jesuitism goes through exercises which lead into the occult life, but into the Will, and within the field of occultism they hold the Will in severe discipline; they ‘break it in’, one might say. And the significant fact is that this discipline of the Will does not arise merely from the surface of life, but from something deeper, because the pupil has been led into the occult, in the way just indicated.

If now, leaving aside the exercises of prayer preparatory to all Jesuit exercises, we consider these occult exercises, at least in their chief points, we find that the pupil has first to call up a vivid Imagination of Christ Jesus as the King of the Worlds — mark this carefully: an Imagination. And no one would be received into the degrees of Jesuitism who had not gone through such exercises, and had not experienced in his soul the transformation which such psychic exercises mean for the whole man. But this Imaginative presentation of Christ Jesus as King of the Worlds has to be preceded by something else. The pupil has to call up for himself, in absolute solitude and seclusion, a picture of man as he was created in the world, and how by falling into sin he incurred the possibility of most terrible punishments. And it is strictly prescribed how one must picture such a man; how if he were left to himself he would incur the utmost of torturing penalties. The rules are extraordinarily severe. With all other concepts or ideas excluded, this picture must live uninterruptedly within the soul of the future Jesuit, the picture of the God-forsaken man, the man exposed to the most fearful punishments, together with the feeling: ‘That am I, since I have come into the world and have forsaken God, and have exposed myself to the possibility of the most fearful punishments.’ This must call forth the fear of being forsaken by God, and detestation of man as he is according to his own nature.

Then, in a further Imagination, over against the picture of the outcast, God-forsaken man, must be set the picture of the God full of pity who then became Christ, and through His acts on earth atones for what man has brought about by forsaking the divine path. In contrast to the Imagination of the God-forsaken man, there must arise that of the all-merciful, loving Being, Christ Jesus, to whom alone it is due that man is not exposed to all possible punishments working upon his soul. And, just as vividly as a feeling of contempt for the forsaking of the divine path had first to become fixed in the soul of the Jesuit pupil, so must a feeling of humility and contrition now take hold of him in the presence of Christ.

When these 2 feelings have been called forth in the pupil, then for several weeks he has to practise severe exercises, picturing to himself in Imagination all details of the life of Jesus from his birth to the Crucifixion and Resurrection. And all that can arise in the soul emerges when the pupil lives in rigorous seclusion and, except for necessary meals, lets nothing else work upon his soul than the pictures which the Gospels give of the compassionate life of Jesus. But these pictures do not merely appear before him in thoughts and ideas; they must work upon his soul in vivid, living Imaginations.

Only someone who really knows how the human soul is transformed through Imaginations which work with full living power — only he knows that under such conditions the soul is in fact completely changed. Such Imaginations, because they are concentrated in the most intense, one-sided way, first on sinful man, secondly on the compassionate God, and then only on the pictures from the New Testament, evoke precisely, through the law of polarity, a strengthened Will. These pictures produce their effect directly, at first hand, for any reflection upon them must be dutifully excluded. It is solely a matter of holding before one's mind these Imaginations, as they have been described.

What then follows is this. In the further exercises Christ Jesus — and now we may no longer say Christ, but exclusively Jesus — is represented as the universal King of the Worlds, and thereby the Jesus element is exaggerated. Because Christ had to be incarnated in a human body, the purely spiritual took part in the physical world; but over against this participation stand the monumental and most significant words: “My kingdom is not of this world.” We can exaggerate the Jesus element by making Jesus into a king of this world, by making Him that which He would have become if He had not resisted the tempter who wished to give Him ‘all the kingdoms of the world and the glory thereof’. Then Jesus of Nazareth would have been a king who, unlike other kinds who possess only a portion of the earth, would have had the whole earth under his sway. If we think of this kind portrayed in this guise, his kingly power so increased that the whole earth is his domain, then we should have the very picture that followed the other exercises through which the personal will of each Jesuit pupil had been sufficiently strengthened.

To prepare for this picture of “King Jesus”, this Ruler over all the kingdoms of the earth, the pupil had to form an Imagination of Babylon and the plain around Babylon as a living picture, and, enthroned over Babylon, Lucifer with his banner. This picture had to be visualized with great exactitude, for it is a powerful imagination: King Lucifer, with his banner and his hosts of Luciferic angels, seated amidst fire and dense smoke, as he sends out his angels to conquer the kingdoms of the earth. And the whole danger that issues from the ‘banner of Lucifer’ must first of all be imagined by itself, without casting a glance upon Christ Jesus. The soul must be entirely engrossed in the Imagination of the danger which issues from the banner of Lucifer. The soul must learn to feel that the greatest danger to the world's existence that could be conjured forth would be a victory for the banner of Lucifer. And when this picture has had its effect, the other Imagination, ‘The banner of Jesus’, must take its place. The pupil must now visualise Jerusalem and the plain around Jerusalem; King Jesus with His hosts, how he conquers and drives off the hosts of Lucifer and makes Himself King of the whole earth — the victory of the banner of Jesus over the banner of Lucifer.

These are the strength-giving Imaginations for the Will which are brought before the soul of the Jesuit pupil. This is what completely changes his Will; makes him such that in his Will, because it is trained occultly, he turns away from everything else and surrenders absolutely to the idea: ‘King Jesus must become the Ruler upon earth, and we who belong to His army have to employ every means to make Him Ruler of the earth. To this we pledge ourselves, we who belong to His host assembled on the plain of Jerusalem, against the host of Lucifer assembled on the plain of Babylon. And the greatest disgrace for a soldier of King Jesus is to forsake His banner.’

These ideas, gathered up into a single resolution of the Will, can certainly give the Will immense strength. But we must ask: what is it in the soul-life that has been directly attacked? The element that ought not to be touched — the Will-element. In so far as this Jesuit training lays hold of the Will-element, while the Jesus-idea seizes the Will-element completely, in so far is the concept of the dominion of Jesus exaggerated in the most dangerous way — dangerous because through it the Will becomes so strong that it can work directly upon the Will of another. For where the Will becomes so strong through Imaginations, which means by occult means, it acquires the capacity for working directly upon the Will of another, and hence also along all the other occult paths to which such a Will can have recourse.

Thus we see how in recent centuries we encounter these two movements, among many others: one has exaggerated the Jesus-element and sees in ‘King Jesus’ the sole ideal of Christianity, which the other looks solely at the Christ-element and carefully sets aside anything that could go beyond it. This second outlook has been much calumniated because it maintains that Christ has sent the Spirit, so that, indirectly through the Spirit, Christ can enter into the hearts and minds of men. In the development of civilisation during the last few centuries there is hardly a greater contrast than that between Jesuitism and Rosicrucianism, for Jesuitism contains nothing of what Rosicrucianism regards as the highest ideal concerning human worth and human dignity, while Rosicrucianism has always sought to guard itself from any influence which could in the remotest sense be called Jesuitical.

In this lecture I wished to show how even so lofty an element as the Jesus-Principle can be exaggerated and then becomes dangerous, and how necessary it is to sink oneself into the depths of the Christ-Being if we wish to understand how the strength of Christianity must reside in esteeming, to the very highest degree, human dignity and human worth, and in strictly refraining from groping our clumsy way into man's inmost sanctuary. Rosicrucianism, even more than Christian mysticism, is attacked by the Jesuit element, because the Jesuits feel that true Christianity is being sought elsewhere than in the setting which offers merely ‘King Jesus’ in the leading role. But the Imaginations here indicated, together with the prescribed exercises, have made the Will so strong that even protests brought against it in the name of the Spirit can be defeated.

JESUIT AND ROSICRUCIAN TRAINING
GA 131
This lecture is in the collected edition of Rudolf Steiner's works;
5 October 1911, Karlsruhe

The movement which interests us in connection with out spiritual-scientific point of view, and which we may call an extraordinarily dangerous error in a certain sense, is the movement known in the external world as Jesuitism. In Jesuitism we encounter a dangerous exaggeration of the Jesus-Principle. In the other movement, which for centuries has existed in Europe as Rosicrucianism, we have an inward Christ-movement which above all seeks carefully for the ways of truth.

Ever since a Jesuitical current arose in Europe, much has been said and written in exoteric life about Jesuitism. Those who wish to study spiritual life from its deeper sources will thus be concerned to see how far Jesuitism signifies a dangerous exaggeration of the Jesus-Principle. If we wish to arrive at a true characterisation of Jesuitism, we must get to know how the three chief principles of world-evolution, which are indicated in the most varied ways in the different world-outlooks, find practical statement in human life, including exoteric life. Today we will first of all turn quite away from the deeper significance and characterisation of these 3 fundamental streams, which run through all life and all evolution, and will review them from an external point of view.

First of all we have the cognitional element in our soul-life. Now, whatever may be said against the abstractions of a one-sided intellectual search for truth, or against the alienation from life of many scientific, philosophical and theosophical endeavors, anyone who is clear in his own mind as to what he wills and what he can will, knows that Cognition belongs to the most deeply rooted activities of the soul. For whether we seek knowledge chiefly through thinking, or more through sensation or feeling, Cognition always signifies a taking account of the world around us, and also of ourselves. Hence we must say that whether we are satisfied for the moment with the simplest experiences of the soul, or whether we wish to devote ourselves to the most complicated analysis of the mysteries of existence, Cognition is the primary and most significant question. For it is basically through Cognition that we form a picture of the content of the world — a picture we live by and from which our entire soul-life is nourished. The very first sense-impression, in fact all sense-life, must be included in the realm of Cognition, along with the highest formulations of the intellect.

Under Cognition we must include also the impulse to distinguish between the beautiful and the ugly, for although it is true in a certain sense that there is no disputing about taste, yet cognition is involved when someone has adopted a certain judgment in a question of taste and can distinguish between the beautiful and the ugly. Again, our moral impulses — those which prompt us to do good and abstain from evil — must be seen as moral ideas, as cognition, or as impulses to do the one and avoid the other. Even what we call our conscience, however vague the impulses from it may be, comes under the heading of Cognition. In short, the world we are consciously aware of, whether it be reality or maya; the world we live in consciously, everything we are conscious of — all this can be embraced under the heading: cognitive spiritual life.

Everyone, however, must acknowledge that under the surface of this cognitive life something else can be discerned; that in our everyday existence our soul-life gives evidence of many things which are not part of our conscious life. When we wake up in the morning, our soul-life if always strengthened and refreshed and newly born from sleep. During the unconsciousness of sleep we have gained something which is outside the realm of conscious cognition, but comes from a region where our soul is active below the level of consciousness.

In waking life, too, we must admit that we are impelled by impulses, instincts and forces which throw up their waves into our conscious life, while they work and have their being below it. We become aware that they work below the conscious when they rise above the surface which separates the conscious from the subconscious soul-life of this kind, for we can see how in the moral realm this or that ideal comes to birth. It takes only a little self-knowledge to realise that these ideals do rise up into our soul-life, but that we are far from always knowing how our great moral ideals are connected with the deepest questions of existence, or how they belong to the will of God, in which they must ultimately be grounded. We might indeed compare our soul-life in its totality with a deep ocean. The depths of this oceanic soul-life throw up waves to the surface, and those that break out into the realm of air, which we can compare with normal consciousness, are brought within the range of conscious cognition. All conscious life is rooted in a subconscious soul-life.

Fundamentally, the whole evolution of mankind can be understood only if a subconscious soul-life of this kind is acknowledged. For what does the progress of spiritual life signify save that many things which have long dwelt down below take form for the first time when they are brought to surface level? So it is, for example, when an inventive idea arises in the form of an impulse towards discovery. Subconscious soul-life, as real as our conscious life, must therefore be recognized as a second element in our life of soul.

If we place this subconscious soul-life in a realm that is at first unknown — but not unknowable — we must contrast it with a third element. This element is immediately apparent to external, exoteric observation, for if we turn our attention to the outer world through our senses, or approach it through our intellect or any form of mental activity, we come to know all sorts of things. But a more exact consideration of every age of cognition compels us to realise that behind everything we can know about the world at large something else lies hidden: something that is certainly not unknowable but in every epoch has to be described as not yet known. And this not-yet-known, which lies below the surface of the known in the mineral, plant and animal kingdoms, belongs as much to ourselves as it does to external nature. It belongs to us in so far as we absorb and work up in our physical organism the materials and forces of the outer world; and inasmuch as we have within us a portion of nature, we have also within us a portion of the unknown in nature. So in the world wherein we live we must distinguish a triad: our conscious spiritual life; our subconscious soul-life below the threshold of consciousness; and that which, as the unknown in nature and at the same time in man, lives in us as part of the great unknown Nature.

Drone strike in Nyala kills at least 21 and injures more than 40

At least 21 people died when a drone struck Tangooj market in Nyala on Monday evening, according to a report from Kenya Today. A medic at Nyala Hospital gave a similar death count and said more than 40 people had been hurt, as reported by Al Jazeera. These accounts therefore place the known death toll at no fewer than 21, while the injury count is above 40 rather than an exact total. The two counts describe different outcomes of the same strike: people reported killed and people reported injured. The reports do not provide a confirmed division of either group between civilians and RSF combatants.

A resident of Nyala told Al Jazeera that the attack occurred at about 8pm on Monday, corresponding in the report to 18:00 GMT. The resident located the market in the city’s northern area, while Kenya Today identified the site as Tangooj market. The hospital medic’s account of 21 deaths and more than 40 injuries was given on Tuesday, according to Al Jazeera. Al Jazeera also said AFP reported the toll, drawing on a medical source and witnesses. The hospital account and the reported AFP tally provide corroboration for the reported scale, but the cited accounts do not supply a final casualty breakdown.

Witnesses said armed people, including RSF fighters, regularly went to the market before it was hit. A separate resident quoted by Al Jazeera also described the market as a place used by armed men, especially RSF members. Those accounts describe who frequented the location; they do not show that any particular armed visitor was among the dead or injured. The available reporting thus establishes the market’s reported use by RSF fighters, while leaving the identities and status of casualties unresolved. That distinction matters when reading a toll that counts deaths and injuries without stating how many were civilians or combatants.

The strike occurred in Nyala, the capital of South Darfur, in southwestern Sudan. The city also has political importance for the Rapid Support Forces, or RSF, which has set up an administration competing with the government based in Khartoum. Al Jazeera characterizes Nyala as the paramilitary group’s practical capital, a description that underscores its role in the RSF’s presence. The rival administration in Nyala is set against the internationally recognised government in Khartoum, according to Al Jazeera. These descriptions concern Nyala’s political position and do not resolve who was harmed in the market.

Sudan’s military has been fighting the RSF since April 2023, according to Al Jazeera. The report from Kenya Today places the market attack after a week in which the army intensified air operations near Nyala International Airport. Those operations targeted RSF positions, command centres and air-defence installations, the same report said. Al Jazeera says the Sudanese military regularly carries out strikes in Nyala, where the RSF has declared its competing administration. The accounts place the market strike within a conflict that includes recurring military attacks on the city, without identifying who launched this particular drone.

Kenya Today reports that drones have increasingly reached places where civilians gather, including markets. That reported pattern gives the Nyala location wider significance, though the accounts do not say how many civilian victims were at Tangooj market. The United Nations reported at least 306 deaths from drone attacks during the first three weeks of October. That figure covers deaths attributed to drone strikes over the stated October period; it is not a count of the injured in Nyala. The reported national figure and the Nyala toll concern different scopes and should not be treated as competing totals for the same event.

The war has caused deaths on a scale described as tens of thousands and has displaced millions, according to Kenya Today. The same account says fighting has disrupted food supplies and aid work across Sudan. These wider effects describe the conflict’s reach beyond the immediate casualties in Nyala, but they do not specify how the market strike changed food access or aid delivery there. The report offers no local breakdown for the people displaced, the supplies disrupted or the aid operations affected by this particular attack.

On Monday, the United States and the European Union called for wider humanitarian access and urgent steps to prevent famine. That appeal addresses humanitarian access and famine risk, while the available facts do not describe a specific aid measure taken in response to the Nyala strike. The request comes amid reported disruption to food and relief operations throughout Sudan. The reports establish a minimum of 21 deaths and more than 40 injuries, but leave the civilian-combatant split uncertain. They also describe RSF fighters as frequent visitors to the market without establishing whether any were among those harmed.

Two Christian Writers recorded the single Event that turned Rome from Persecutor to Patron of the Church, and even they couldn't agree on what Constantine actually saw.

Lactantius, writing closest to the Event, describes only a Dream the Night before the Battle, Constantine instructed to mark his Soldiers' Shields with a Heavenly Sign, likely the Chi-Rho, the first two Letters of Christ's Name in Greek.

Eusebius, writing Decades later as Constantine's own Biographer, tells a far grander Story: Constantine and his entire Army witnessed a Cross Of Light suspended directly over the Sun itself, inscribed with the Words "Εν Τούτῳ Νίκα" (In This [Sign], Conquer!), followed that same Night by Christ Himself appearing in a Dream to explain it.

Here's where honest Skepticism earns its place, Constantine had already been a Devotee of Sol Invictus, the Unconquered Sun, and a Pagan Orator two Years earlier described him receiving a Vision of Apollo at a Gallic Shrine.

A Solar Halo Phenomenon, three Suns producing a Cross-Shaped Optical Effect, offers one Natural Explanation for what the Soldiers might have seen in the Sky that Day.

Whoever, some Scholars say that Eusebius, writing as Constantine's own Court Historian long after the Emperor held Absolute Power over the now-favored Church, had every Political Incentive to elevate a Private Dream into a Public Cosmic Sign witnessed by Thousands.

None of that automatically disqualifies a Genuine Theophany, though, God working through Military Victory, confirmed by a Vision, and later Theologically amplified by an admiring Biographer, isn't a “contradiction”. 

It's precisely how Ancient Historiography usually operated.

Whether God broke directly into History that Morning, or a grieving Church simply needed its Deliverer wrapped in Heaven's own Light, the outcome reshaped Western Civilization permanently either way.

It seems far more likely that both Lactantius and Eusebius were both telling the truth and that Constantine had both a Dream and later experienced a Theophantic Vision as well.

This a genuinely reasonable hrmonization, and it's not even a novel one — some Historians studying the Sources read the Evidence exactly this way.

The Chronology actually supports it well where the Pagan Orator's Speech describing Constantine's Vision of Apollo dates to 310 A.D., two full Years before the Milvian Bridge.

If that Vision was real, it would represent an Earlier Stage in Constantine's own Spiritual Journey, still operating within a Pagan Solar Framework centered on Sol Invictus and Apollo, the Dominant Devotion of his own Father Constantius before him.

Then, by 312 A.D., as Constantine faced a Decisive Battle with everything at stake, a second, more specifically Christian Experience could very plausibly follow, Lactantius's immediate, sparser Report of a Dream instructing him toward the Chi-Rho, and Eusebius's fuller Account, drawn directly from what Constantine told him personally Decades later, recalling the Cross in the Sky and Christ's Own Explanation that Night.

Read this way, the three Accounts stop competing and start forming an actual Narrative Arc: a Man already primed by Years of Solar Devotion to interpret a dramatic Celestial Sign spiritually, who then received increasing Spiritual Clarity that the Sign pointed specifically toward Christ rather than Apollo. 

The Earlier Pagan Vision wouldn't discredit the later Christian one.

It would explain why Constantine was spiritually prepared to recognize and act on it at all.

This actually strengthens the case for a Genuine Theophany rather than pure Political Theater.

A single, isolated Vision conveniently timed to a Power Grab looks more like Propaganda.

A Documented, Multi-Year Spiritual Trajectory, moving in one consistent direction toward increasing Christian Clarity, looks considerably more like an actual Soul being gradually reeled in by Divine Providence.

text:
THE SAGE

PRIDE

Despising Our Rivers of Healing

An unprecedentedly decorated General in the Syrian Army, his reputation as a fierce warrior and a consummate leader of men preceded him. The battlefield was his dinner table, and the spoils of war were his delectable oysters. He relished victory, and victory seemed to relish him. 

In a singularly epochal career that would later qualify as one of the most phenomenally remarkable monuments to military accomplishment, an uninterrupted series of spectacular victories in battles had all but earned him the reputation of one of his era’s most successful war commanders. Not unnaturally, he wore his general’s epaulettes with pride. Unfortunately, that pride almost became his undoing at a moment of critical personal need. 

Naaman was Commander-In-Chief of the Syrian Army. He was powerful, respected, and wealthy. Under his command, officers and men could fight and prevail over any enemy. There was, however, just one enemy his soldiers couldn't fight. General Naaman was afflicted with leprosy. That terrible skin condition was the only blight on an otherwise brilliant life and Naaman was sorely distressed by it. 

A young girl, taken captive by his army from Israel, served as housemaid to Naaman’s wife.
“I know of a prophet in Samaria. He can cure your husband of his leprosy,” she told her mistress. 
Naaman approached his master, the King of Syria, and told him what his wife’s housemaid had said.
“By all means, go,” King Ben-Hadad II replied, “I will send a letter to the King of Israel.” 

Naaman left for Israel, armed with a royal dispatch that read, “With this letter I am sending my servant Naaman to you so that you may cure him of his leprosy.”
The King of Israel fretted that the Syrian King, an adversary whose might and power he was yet to match, had placed an impossible burden on him, since he had no healing power.

At that time, however, there lived in Israel a prophet and miracle worker named Elisha. Upon learning of the untenable situation in which the Israelite king found himself, he offered to heal Naaman of his affliction. On arrival at Elisha’s house, a messenger from the prophet received the general.
“Go and wash yourself seven times in the Jordan River, and you will be healed of your leprosy.”

General Naaman flew into a rage. He couldn’t believe his ears!
“Do you expect someone of my status to wash in that dirty river? Are the rivers of Damascus not better than all the waters of Israel? Couldn’t I wash in them and be cleansed? Prepare my horses! I am leaving!”

One of Naaman’s servants gingerly approached the general. 
“My father, if the prophet asked you to do something difficult, wouldn't you do it? How much more when he simply says, ‘wash and be clean!’”

The counsel of a lowly servant, as is often the case with the high and mighty, did the trick. Naaman went and dipped himself in the Jordan River seven times as the prophet had instructed and his flesh, now restored, became clean like that of a newborn baby. 

The man who had nearly gone back home in righteous offense returned a healed man. More often than not, the biggest obstacle between us and our miracle is neither the devil nor our fellow man. It is usually our pride. We hanker after a spectacular instruction. We crave only that which lends itself to irrefutable logic.

The spectacular irony, however, is that the instruction that will activate a remarkable transformation in our life will often appear too simple for our status. Naaman almost carried his sickness back home just because the solution offered offended his pride. We must insist on not allowing pride to make us despise our rivers of healing, or reject our windows of opportunity. So help us God.

Yomi Garnett MD

Details: https://t.co/OieMk7bRmn

Researchers chained several small flaws in Cloudflare’s image feature. Kevin Gervot and Adam Kues published the work on October 28, 2026, in a write-up titled Cache Me If You Can. 

They showed a working cross-site scripting (XSS) bug through the /cdn-cgi/image/ endpoint on cloudflare.]com. The write-up does not list a CVE or a patch status, so readers should check with Cloudflare.

An attacker can hide a quote mark in that value and break out of it. The filter has already approved the file by then, so the script tag slips through. Cloudflare serves these images with a strict policy of default-src 'none', which blocks scripts.

text:
FALL of BABYLON - a VISION
by Darren Smith (June '09)

{Darren runs a ministry to the homeless in Texas, USA}.

The Lord kept me up most of the night, bringing a word for me to share and to share now. Many times I wait until I have prayed over what I hear in my spirit, but I can't wait to send this word out.

Last night while praying before I went to bed, the Lord gave me a vision that really rattled me. In the vision I saw this land split into four parts, with each one under its own flag. Each region had terrible destruction, and many people were dead. As I looked over the
destruction; I was crying, and the Lord asked me, "Why are you crying over the fall of Babylon? As a matter of fact, why have you been praying for the healing of Babylon?"

In this vision I didn't have an answer, and the Lord opened a scroll and started reading off the indictments against our country, but before each one he clearly called the USA Babylon.

The list was long and to the point, with such points as the killing of several generations of unborn children. Beside this charge He added that these babies had been sacrificed to the god of self. The list also included greed, idolatry, pride, fornication, and many others;
so many I could not even read them all.

As I looked at the list of charges, I was overwhelmed and broken by the fact that we live every day in a nation that is so far removed from God and in total opposition to the Kingdom of God, yet we are comfortable here. We have become just like Lot living in Sodom, the prosperity that the nation offers us has blinded us from the evil
that rules this land. We complain about how bad it is but still stay attached to it with every ounce of strength we have.

The Lord told me to look at the nation as He sees it, not through my eyes but through His. I could not look too long before I had to agree and repent of loving Babylon. Once I repented, the Lord told me to prepare for the fall as time is running out. I must preach the Gospel of The Kingdom not the Gospel of America. America is already judged; the time of shaking is now and will increase rapidly this summer. Water shortages and food shortages will become common this summer, as well as fuel shortages. Civil unrest will become common place in large cities first but will spill over into the rural areas as well.

Natural disasters will stretch the resources of the nation to the breaking point and the government will use this to take freedom away. Brothers up north take note, you will see this start to happen quickly. Please seek the Lord for direction as you are out of time. The west coast will see this soon as well, please prepare.

Rescuers continued searching the wreckage as Spain began three days of mourning.

The United States warned Middle Eastern allies to prepare for possible renewed strikes against Iran after the November 3 midterm elections, and for Iranian retaliation against energy facilities and other critical infrastructure. President Trump has not made a final decision. Meanwhile, Qatari mediators presented Tehran with a proposed seven-day sequence of steps intended to end the eight-month war. Protest movements involving students, unions and anti-government groups continued across Europe. Swamiji [Vivekananda] visited the Chhatrapati family Deity temple, Maa Bhavani Devi, and also went to Mahalakshmi Devi temple [at Kolhapur in 1892 during his itinerant days] and paid obeisance. He became ecstatic standing in the inner sanctum of the temple and prostrated before her.

... After hearing about Swamiji's personality and erudition, she [Rani Anandibai, queen of Kolhapur] expressed her wish to meet him. The secretary immediately sent a messenger with a letter to Swamiji. The letter said: 'Swamiji, the Rani wishes to meet you. Since she is not well, she will not be able to go to Khasbag. She will feel most obliged if you kindly come to her palace.' As soon as Swamiji received the letter, he made his way towards the palace. The Chhatrapati was always respectful towards sadhus. The Rani was impressed to see Swamiji and paid obeisance to him. She thought all the problems of her life would be resolved after receiving the blessings of such a divine personality. She shared her troubles with him and sought peace.

Swamiji said: 'Mother, you can get peace only by thinking of God. My Guru said that God is everywhere but He is more visible in man. Therefore the highest spirituality is to serve man and that is the best and easiest way to worship God.' The Rani was filled with gratitude to hear this and she sought 'mantra diksha' (initiation) from him. On the third day, Anandibai received her mantra... 

After receiving mantra diksha from Swamiji, Anandibai offered gold, diamond, jewellery and many other valuables on a silver plate at his feet. Seeing them, Swamiji said: 'Mother, I am a begging sannyasi, I don't need all these things, and I can't accept them.' Anandibai was disappointed and began to feel helpless. With a heavy heart she said, 'Gurudev! I received mahamantra, and shall feel hurt if you don't receive any dakshina (offering).'

Observing his disciple's feelings, Swamiji said:
 'Mother, you may offer a saffron cloth to me.' Anandibai at once instructed her secretary to make arrangements for it. 
In the meantime, Anandibai noticed that Swamiji's shoes were absolutely worn out. She told her secretary to preserve his old pair of shoes and to put a pair of Kolhapuri sandals on his feet. When the secretary followed the Rani's instructions, Swamiji did not refuse.

Later, Rani Anandibai gave up her 'Rajmata' title and transformed herself to 'Mother of all'. She started a school for untouchable boys and girls of Kolhapur. She made ponds and started an orphanage for them. Swamiji's influence could be felt in all her work. Keeping Swamiji in her mind always, Maharani Anandi Bai passed away in 1902.

- "Indian Women In the Company of Swami Vivekananda" by Tarit Kumar Bandyopadhyay, Page 118 - 119.

text:
PART TWO: THE COSMIC VOICE — FROM DIVINE INTENTION TO MANIFESTATION

4. Thoth, the Architect of Understanding

Ancient Egyptian traditions describe Nun as the primordial waters of potential, from which creation emerges. Different traditions name different creators, including Atum, Ptah, and Thoth. In the Hermopolitan tradition, Thoth represents wisdom, sacred speech, writing, calculation, and cosmic order.

Symbolically, Thoth makes existence understandable. Like an architect who designs a temple before its construction, thought establishes the plan before the hands bring it into reality.

5. The Seven Vowels as Principles of Creation

The seven Greek vowels can be interpreted symbolically as stages of cosmic order:

- Alpha: The beginning of embodied life.
- Epsilon: Communication and the exchange of meaning.
- Eta: Relationships, balance, and proportion.
- Iota: Awareness and recognition.
- Omicron: Change and transformation.
- Upsilon: The organisation of complexity through higher principles.
- Omega: Completion, limitation, and return to mystery.

This is a philosophical interpretation, not a proven ancient Egyptian formula. Its central idea is that existence becomes understandable through life, communication, harmony, awareness, transformation, order, and completion.

6. Sacred Geometry: Sound and Measurement

Ancient Egyptian temples demonstrate sophisticated knowledge of mathematics, proportion, symmetry, and orientation. Their construction required practical skills, tools, materials, and careful planning.

Sound and geometry share an important connection: both involve patterns and relationships. Musical tones depend on frequencies, while geometric forms depend on lengths, angles, and proportions. Cymatics demonstrates how vibrations can create visible patterns in certain materials.

However, this does not prove that vowels create atoms or that planetary systems originate from specific sounds. Symbolically, sound reveals patterns, mathematics describes relationships, and geometry gives those relationships visible form.

7. As Above, So Below

The Hermetic maxim “As above, so below” expresses the idea that different levels of reality may reflect related patterns. It is a spiritual principle, not an established scientific law.

The seven planetary associations offer a symbolic guide to human experience:

- Moon: Bodily rhythms.
- Mercury: Thought and communication.
- Venus: Relationships and attraction.
- Sun: Awareness and vitality.
- Mars: Action and courage.
- Jupiter: Wisdom and expansion.
- Saturn: Discipline and limitation.

These associations encourage reflection on the relationship between the cosmos and human life without claiming that planetary influences are scientifically proven.

8. Returning to the Source

Some Hermetic texts describe spiritual understanding as a journey beyond the seven planetary spheres toward higher knowledge of the divine. The Discourse on the Eighth and Ninth explores this expanded spiritual vision, while other Hermetic writings use vowel sequences in prayers and hymns.

The deeper journey is from instinct to understanding, confusion to order, and attachment to contemplation of the divine.

Thoth symbolises the union of perception, language, measurement, and wisdom. Speech without understanding becomes noise; knowledge without balance creates disorder; and craftsmanship without vision lacks direction.

The hammer builds the temple, but the mind conceives its design. The tongue expresses thought, writing preserves it, and the hands transform it into reality.

The cosmic voice therefore represents the movement from divine intention to ordered manifestation—not a scientifically proven mechanism by which seven vowels physically create the universe.
